Mobile County by the numbers

What is Mobile County, Alabama, and how is it laid out?

Mobile County is the state's southwestern corner, a Gulf Coast county of 414,809 people at the 2020 census and the third most populous county in Alabama. Its seat and largest city is Mobile, which is also the second largest city in the state.

The county was organized on December 18, 1812, and it covers 1,644 square miles, of which 415 square miles (25.2%) is water. It takes in islands including Dauphin Island, Gaillard Island and Mon Louis Island, and that much shoreline shapes everything from insurance to flood maps to what a house is worth.

Mobile County factFigure
County organizedDecember 18, 1812
Total area1,644 square miles (415 water)
Population, 2020 census414,809
Households, 2020 census163,750
Housing units184,441, with 11.2% vacant
Owner-occupied share of occupied homes64.6%

Mobile County and Washington County together make up the Mobile metropolitan area, and adding the Daphne-Fairhope-Foley area produces a combined statistical area with a 2020 population of 661,964.

Which cities and communities are in Mobile County?

Mobile County has nine incorporated cities, two towns and a long list of unincorporated communities. The cities are Bayou La Batre, Chickasaw, Citronelle, Creola, Mobile, Prichard, Saraland, Satsuma and Semmes, and the towns are Dauphin Island and Mount Vernon.

  • Census-designated places: Axis, Belle Fontaine, Bucks, Calvert, Chunchula, Grand Bay, Gulfcrest, Movico, Theodore and Tillmans Corner.
  • Unincorporated communities include Coden, Eight Mile, Irvington, Kushla, Mon Louis, St. Elmo, Tanner Williams, Whistler and Wilmer.
  • School systems: the Mobile County Public School System covers most areas, while Chickasaw, Saraland and Satsuma run their own.

A house in Saraland, one in Theodore and one on Dauphin Island all sit in the same county, but the millage and school levy on each can differ. Check which taxing districts the parcel belongs to before you trust any estimate you find online.

Who handles property tax in Mobile County?

The Mobile County Revenue Commission assesses and collects property tax for the county, and its offices are closed on Wednesdays. That closing day catches people out, especially near the end of the year when lines are longest.

The commission's own personal property page repeats the state calendar: taxes are due October 1 and turn delinquent on January 1. If you own rental houses with appliances or furnishings, or a business that keeps equipment at a house, note that personal property must be listed after October 1 and no later than December 31. Listing late past the third Monday in January adds a 10% penalty plus fees.

For homes, the practical contact is the Revenue Commission for assessment and billing, and the county probate office for recording the deed. Keep those two straight when you sell.

The Mobile County Revenue Commission site is the place to find locations and forms.

When does Mobile County property tax become delinquent?

Property tax in Mobile County is due October 1 and delinquent after December 31, following the state calendar. The Alabama Department of Revenue timetable then moves to February for the probate court handoff, April for newspaper advertising and May for a tax sale.

MonthStep in the state timetable
October 1Taxes due
January 1Taxes delinquent
FebruaryTurned over to probate court
MarchProbate court meets
AprilAdvertised for sale
MayTax sale

An owner who knows a bill is unpaid has until December 31 to clear it without the delinquency process starting. After that the clock in the table starts. If you plan to sell, the best time to act is before January.

What does Mobile County's climate mean for a house?

Mobile County has a mild, humid subtropical climate, and a 2007 study named Mobile the wettest city in the contiguous 48 states, with 66.3 inches of average annual rainfall over 30 years. Water is the first thing a buyer or inspector will look at, which means roofs, drainage, crawl spaces and flood zones matter more here than in most places.

Hurricanes are part of the county's history. Frederic, a Category 3 storm, passed over Mobile on September 12, 1979. Hurricane Ivan struck on September 16, 2004, and Katrina on August 29, 2005 brought an 11.45 foot storm surge that flooded downtown and the Battleship Parkway. In 2020 Hurricane Sally was the first hurricane since Ivan to directly hit Alabama, and Zeta followed a month later as a Category 3.

Owners of houses with storm damage that was only partly repaired can sell to a cash buyer in the current condition, without finishing the work first.

How do roads, ports and jobs shape Mobile County housing?

Mobile County is crossed by Interstate 10, Interstate 65 and Interstate 165, along with U.S. Highways 43, 45, 90 and 98, and The Wave Transit System serves the area. The county is home to Alabama's only deepwater port, and Mobile's port ranks as the 12th largest in the United States.

Major industries in the city of Mobile include aerospace, steel, shipbuilding, retail, services, construction, medicine and manufacturing. Austal USA began shipbuilding in 1999, an Airbus A320 family assembly plant opened in Mobile in 2015, and the Mobile Aeroplex at Brookley hosts more than 70 companies on 1,650 acres.

The University of South Alabama, Spring Hill College and the University of Mobile are all in the county, and the county's 2020 census count shows 35.4% of occupied homes are rented.

How do you appeal or pay property tax when selling a Mobile County house?

Appeals start with a written challenge to the valuation through the county Board of Equalization, and a ruling from that board can then be appealed to circuit court within 30 days. Alabama Code 40-3-25 requires notice to the board secretary and the circuit clerk, plus a bond, and says the taxpayer must pay the prior year's tax before it becomes delinquent or risk dismissal.

At closing, a title company or closing attorney normally collects the payoff for any unpaid tax from the seller's proceeds. The deed goes to the probate court for recording, and Alabama Code 40-22-1 sets the deed tax at $0.50 for each $500 of value. On a $120,000 sale that deed tax is $120.

  • Get a current balance from the Revenue Commission before you list or accept an offer.
  • Check the parcel for exemptions that need to be released or reclaimed.
  • Gather the paperwork for any inherited property, since the deed chain must be clean.
  • Ask the title company how it will handle a lien from an earlier year.

What do Mobile County sellers usually face?

Mobile County sellers often deal with storm-worn roofs, older housing and estates. In the city of Mobile, the Census count of 2020 was 187,041, and Mobile has many historic neighborhoods including Ashland Place, Oakleigh Garden, Old Dauphin Way and Spring Hill. Houses in older neighborhoods like these often need more upkeep than newer ones.

Another group owns houses in areas hit by past storms, such as the eastern sections of Mobile that flooded during Katrina. A third group inherited a house and cannot afford the repairs and back tax at once.

Cash Home Buyers buys houses in Mobile County as-is, including those with tax due, so the seller does not pay for repairs before closing. Any unpaid property tax is taken from the proceeds by the title company.

More questions about Mobile County, AL Property Tax Guide

When is Mobile County property tax due?

Property tax is due October 1 and delinquent after December 31. The Mobile County Revenue Commission collects it.

Is the Mobile County Revenue Commission open on Wednesdays?

No. The commission's site says all of its offices are closed on Wednesdays, so plan visits for other weekdays.

What happens if I do not pay Mobile County property tax?

After December 31 the bill is delinquent. The state timetable then sends it to probate court in February, advertises it in April, and holds a tax sale in May.

How long do I have to appeal an assessment in Mobile County?

A written appeal goes to the Board of Equalization. An appeal of the board's decision to circuit court must be taken within 30 days under Alabama Code 40-3-25.

Can I sell a Mobile County house that has back property tax?

Yes. The title company pays the back tax from the sale proceeds at closing, so ask the Revenue Commission for a balance first.

Baldwin County by the numbers

Where is Baldwin County, Alabama, and how is it laid out?

Baldwin County sits in the southwestern corner of Alabama on the Gulf coast, on the eastern side of Mobile Bay. According to its Wikipedia entry, it is the largest county in the state by area, at 2,027 square miles in total, of which 1,590 are land. The county seat is Bay Minette, while Daphne is the largest city.

Locals describe the county in regions: North Baldwin, the Eastern Shore, Central Baldwin, South Baldwin, Southwest Baldwin and East Baldwin. Central Baldwin is the strip along State Route 59 from the Interstate 10 exit at Loxley through Robertsdale to Summerdale. The Census Bureau splits the county into subdivisions centered on Bay Minette, Daphne, Elberta, Fairhope, Foley, Robertsdale, Stockton and Summerdale.

FactDetail
EstablishedDecember 21, 1809
County seatBay Minette
Largest cityDaphne
2020 census population231,767
2025 estimate on the same page267,761
Metro areaDaphne-Fairhope-Foley

If you own a house here, the first thing to know is which of these areas it is in. The county has three public school districts: Baldwin County, Gulf Shores City and Orange Beach City, the last formed in 2022. A house in Orange Beach and one in Bay Minette are in the same county but not the same school system.

What cities and towns are in Baldwin County?

The county lists nine cities and five towns. The cities are Bay Minette, Daphne, Fairhope, Foley, Gulf Shores, Loxley, Orange Beach, Robertsdale and Spanish Fort. The towns are Elberta, Magnolia Springs, Perdido Beach, Silverhill and Summerdale.

There are also unincorporated places and census designated places such as Point Clear, Fort Morgan, Bon Secour, Lillian, Stapleton and Stockton. Check your tax bill to see which levies apply to your address.

  • The Foley subdivision includes Gulf Shores, Magnolia Springs and most of Orange Beach.
  • The Daphne subdivision includes Spanish Fort.
  • The Robertsdale subdivision includes Loxley and Silverhill.
  • The Elberta subdivision includes Perdido Beach.

How fast has Baldwin County grown, and what does that mean for a house seller?

Baldwin was Alabama's fastest-growing county from 2010 to 2020, per the same source, and four of the state's ten fastest-growing cities were in it. The population went from 182,265 in 2010 to 231,767 in 2020. Of the 124,148 housing units counted in the 2020 census, 25.0 percent were vacant.

Growth is uneven. The Foley subdivision grew from 48,089 to 64,862 people between 2010 and 2020, and the Daphne subdivision, which includes Spanish Fort, went from 41,295 to 55,767. The Stockton area was nearly flat, at 3,804 and 3,745.

For a seller, that spread means two different markets under one county name. Check the numbers for your own part of the county rather than the county average. Our cash offers reflect the condition and location of the specific house.

What is the climate risk for a Baldwin County house?

Baldwin frequently endures tropical weather systems, and the county has been declared a disaster area several times. Wikipedia lists Hurricane Frederic in September 1979, Danny in July 1997, Georges in September 1998, Ivan in September 2004, Katrina in August 2005 and Sally in September 2020.

That history shapes what a buyer looks at on a coastal house: roof condition, wind and flood coverage, drainage and any storm repair that is half done. A property that has been through a named storm and has an open insurance claim or unrepaired damage is a very different sale from a tidy one.

Cash sales are one way owners avoid the delay of repair loans, appraisals tied to condition, and buyers who back out after an inspection. We purchase houses as they stand, including storm-damaged ones.

How do roads, schools and airports shape a Baldwin County sale?

Interstate 10 and Interstate 65 cross the county, along with U.S. Highways 31, 90 and 98 and State Routes 59, 104, 180, 181, 182, 225 and 287. The Baldwin Beach Express is also listed. Loxley is described as growing as a suburb of Daphne and Spanish Fort because it has an Interstate 10 exit and sits roughly between Mobile and Pensacola.

The county has airports at Bay Minette, Fairhope, Foley and Gulf Shores, but commercial scheduled service comes from Mobile Regional Airport, Mobile Downtown Airport or Pensacola International Airport. Coastal Alabama Community College has several campuses in the county, and the United States Sports Academy is in Daphne.

Part of Wolf Bay and 42 miles of the Tensaw River were designated Outstanding Alabama Water, and part of the Bon Secour National Wildlife Refuge lies in the county. If your house is near water, keep your survey and any flood certificate handy.

How is property tax handled by the Baldwin County Revenue Commission?

Baldwin has an elected revenue commissioner who serves the whole county. The Collections Division collects tax on all real and personal property assessed in the county, and its page says taxes are due October 1 each year. Courtesy notices usually go out before then so owners can check their mailing address.

Taxes are delinquent after December 31. Penalties and interest begin to accrue after that date, and the owner has to contact Collections to learn the new amount due. Personal and business checks are accepted between October 1 and February 28. The collections phone number on the page is 251-937-0245.

If a mortgage company pays your tax through escrow, the page says it is still the owner's responsibility to confirm the payment was made. The county offers an EscrowCheck tool that shows the real-time status of escrow payments from banks and lenders, using the parcel number without dashes.

  • October 1: taxes due.
  • December 31: last day before delinquency.
  • February 28: last day for personal and business checks.

How do you protest a Baldwin County property valuation?

The Revenue Commission's FAQ lists questions on how to protest an appraised value, whether a protest can be filed by phone, what happens if you miss your hearing, and why you might not have received a valuation notice. It also links to a fillable online protest form. The FAQ page collapses the answers, so open it and expand the questions for the current instructions.

One question on that page is worth quoting by topic: the valuation notice is not your tax bill. Owners sometimes mix the two. A notice states the appraised value and starts the protest clock, while the bill arrives for the October 1 due date.

If you plan to sell, do not let an appraisal protest wait. A buyer's title company will want the tax record current, and a pending protest can leave the amount unsettled at closing.

What happens in Baldwin County when taxes go unpaid?

The Revenue Commission's tax lien auction page explains that Alabama's 2018 legislature passed Act 2018-577, an alternative to selling the property: selling the tax lien. Baldwin migrated to lien sales in 2019 beginning with tax year 2018 delinquent properties. All liens for unpaid and delinquent real property taxes are subject to a public auction.

The county's FAQ list for that auction asks the questions an owner would ask. Is ownership transferred when a lien is bought? How do you redeem a lien? What happens to liens that do not sell? The auction uses the GovEase platform, and the page lists one question on whether training is available for it. The answers are on the county page, so read them before you decide anything.

State redemption rules still matter. Our Alabama tax sale page summarizes who can redeem and how long they have.

How does a cash sale work in Baldwin County with tax due?

The title company pays the delinquent tax, and any lien redemption amount, from your proceeds at closing. You supply the parcel number, the tax years owed and a payoff figure from Collections.

If the county sold a lien on your parcel, ask Collections what the payoff includes. Request the figure in writing, and give the title company enough time to confirm it.

We buy Baldwin County houses as they are, including ones with delinquent tax, storm damage or deferred repairs.

More questions about Baldwin County, AL Property Tax Guide

When are Baldwin County property taxes due?

October 1 each year. They become delinquent after December 31, and penalties and interest accrue after that date.

Who collects property tax in Baldwin County?

The Baldwin County Revenue Commission's Collections Division. Its page lists 251-937-0245 as the collections phone number.

What if my mortgage company pays my Baldwin County tax?

Confirm that it did. The Revenue Commission says that is the owner's responsibility, and its EscrowCheck tool shows whether an escrow payment reached the county.

Does Baldwin County sell tax liens or the property itself?

Liens. The Revenue Commission says it began selling tax liens in 2019 with tax year 2018 delinquents under Act 2018-577, and all liens for unpaid real property taxes are subject to public auction.

What is the county seat of Baldwin County?

Bay Minette. Daphne is the largest city, and the county sits on the eastern side of Mobile Bay.

Can I sell a Baldwin County house with unpaid tax?

Yes, in many cases. The tax and any lien payoff are paid from the proceeds at closing, so get a payoff figure from the Collections Division first.

Etowah County by the numbers

Where is Etowah County, Alabama?

Etowah County is in northeast Alabama, with Gadsden as the county seat and largest city. It is the smallest county in Alabama by area, at 549 square miles of which 14 are water, yet it ranks among the most densely populated.

DeKalb County lies to the north, Cherokee to the east, Calhoun to the southeast, St. Clair to the southwest, Blount to the west and Marshall to the northwest. Etowah County makes up the Gadsden metropolitan statistical area.

Wikipedia says the name comes from a Cherokee word meaning 'edible tree' and marks that gloss as needing a citation. The county has 56.8 percent of residents in urban areas and 43.2 percent in rural ones.

Why was Etowah County created twice?

The legislature first established Baine County on December 7, 1866, naming Gadsden as the seat. The state constitutional convention of 1868 abolished it and replaced it on December 1, 1868 with Etowah County, covering the same ground.

Most of the land had earlier belonged to DeKalb and Cherokee counties. The change matters to title researchers, because a very old record from the 1860s may carry the Baine County name.

How many people and homes does Etowah County have?

The 2020 census counted 103,436 people in Etowah County, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 103,886. The county has hovered near 100,000 residents since 1980.

MeasureEtowah County figure
Population, 2020 census103,436
Population estimate, 2025103,886
Households41,974
Housing units47,306
Share of units vacant11.3%
Owner-occupied71.1%
Renter-occupied28.9%
Median age42.4 years
Residents aged 65 or older19.9%

These are 2020 census figures reproduced on Wikipedia. About 29 percent of occupied homes are rented. Population peaked in the 1980 census at 103,057 and again in the 2010 census at 104,430.

What do Etowah County households look like?

Of the 41,974 households counted in 2020, 29.0 percent had children under 18 and 29.2 percent were one person living alone. Another 13.8 percent were someone aged 65 or older living by themselves.

The homeowner vacancy rate was 1.7 percent and the rental vacancy rate was 10.1 percent. Population stood at 93,892 in 1950, 96,980 in 1960 and 94,144 in 1970, so the county has been roughly flat for decades. The 2020 census also found 47,306 housing units, which is about 5,300 more than the number of households.

Which towns and cities are in Etowah County?

Etowah County has seven cities and five towns, plus census-designated and unincorporated places.

  • Cities: Attalla, Boaz (partly in Marshall County), Gadsden, Glencoe (partly in Calhoun County), Hokes Bluff, Rainbow City and Southside (partly in Calhoun County).
  • Towns: Altoona, Reece City, Ridgeville, Sardis City and Walnut Grove.
  • Census-designated places: Ballplay, Bristow Cove, Egypt, Gallant, Ivalee, Lookout Mountain, New Union, Tidmore Bend and Whitesboro.

Alabama City is listed as a former city, so older records may use that name.

Which school districts serve Etowah County?

Four districts cover the county. Etowah County Schools serves the areas outside the city limits of Attalla, Boaz and Gadsden.

  • Attalla City School District
  • Boaz City School District
  • Gadsden City School District
  • Etowah County Schools for everything else

Gadsden State Community College has a campus in the county. A house on the line between a city and the county system should be checked against the district map before a listing claims a school.

How do people travel around Etowah County?

Interstate 59 runs through the county, with I-759 as a spur into Gadsden. U.S. routes 11, 278, 411 and 431 serve the towns, and state routes 77, 132, 179, 205, 211 and 291 fill in the remainder.

Gadsden has a trolley system, and Greyhound Lines operates intercity bus service. Freight rail comes from the Alabama and Tennessee River Railway and Norfolk Southern Railway.

What tornado history should Etowah County sellers know?

An F4 tornado struck the county on Palm Sunday, March 27, 1994, and destroyed Goshen United Methodist Church in Piedmont. Wikipedia says it hit twelve minutes after the National Weather Service issued a warning.

A seller with storm repairs in the history of the house should have the invoices and permits ready for the buyer or title company.

When are Etowah County property taxes due?

Etowah County's own FAQ states that taxes are due October 1 and delinquent on January 1. The county posts the full calendar.

  • October 1: tax due
  • January 1: tax delinquent
  • February: turned over to Probate Court
  • March: Probate Court meets
  • April: advertised for sale
  • May: tax sale

The Revenue Commissioner is not required to mail tax notices and does so as a courtesy, so a missing statement does not excuse a late payment. Payment can be made by mail, in person at the county tax office, or through a mortgage company.

What penalty applies to late Etowah County taxes?

Interest and penalty run at 12 percent a year on past due taxes, according to the county FAQ. Property is sold yearly for unpaid taxes.

An owner has 3 years from the sale to redeem by paying the taxes, interest, fees and penalties at the same 12 percent rate. Paying someone else's taxes does not give a person ownership, and the buyer of a house inherits any unpaid prior years because taxes follow the property.

What exemptions can an Etowah County homeowner claim?

Questions about appraised value go to the Revenue Commissioner, whose office is in the County Courthouse. The regular homestead exemption can be claimed on a principal residence regardless of age or income. It exempts $4,000 of assessed value for state tax and $2,000 for county tax.

  • Homestead II: over 65, blind or totally disabled, with taxable income of $7,500 to $12,000, exempt from state tax and $5,000 of county tax.
  • Homestead III: over 65, blind or totally disabled, with taxable income below $7,500, exempt from all property tax.
  • Homestead IV: same group with income above $12,000, exempt from county tax up to $2,000.

Exemptions must be applied for between October 1 and the third Monday in January, but regular homesteads can be claimed all year. Types II, III and IV need a yearly signed filing with tax returns.

What are the assessment ratios in Etowah County?

Alabama sets four classes. The county FAQ lists them as 30 percent for utilities, 20 percent for all other property, 10 percent for farm, forest and owner-occupied property, and 15 percent for motor vehicles.

On a house valued at $100,000, an owner-occupant is assessed on $10,000 and a landlord on $20,000, before any millage is applied.

What should a buyer or seller do at the Etowah County courthouse?

The county advises a buyer to record the deed in the Probate Office and then assess the property at the Revenue Commissioner's office, bringing the deed along. It also warns buyers to get a title opinion first, because delinquent taxes follow the property.

Recording privilege tax is fifty cents per $500 of value under Alabama Code 40-22-1, so a $140,000 sale carries $140 plus the recording fee.

More questions about Etowah County, AL Property Tax Guide

What is the county seat of Etowah County, Alabama?

Gadsden, which is also the largest city, according to Wikipedia. The county courthouse in Gadsden also houses the Revenue Commissioner's office, where assessments are handled.

When are Etowah County property taxes due?

October 1, delinquent January 1, with a tax sale in May, according to the Etowah County tax FAQ.

How much interest applies to late taxes in Etowah County?

Twelve percent a year on past due taxes, per the county's published FAQ.

Can I redeem a property sold for taxes in Etowah County?

Yes, within 3 years of the sale, by paying taxes, interest, fees and penalties at 12 percent a year.

Do I get the Etowah County homestead exemption automatically?

No. It has to be claimed with the Revenue Commissioner. The regular homestead can be claimed year round on a principal residence.

Where is Lauderdale County and what is in it?

Lauderdale County occupies the northwest corner of Alabama, with Florence as its seat and largest city. The Tennessee River forms its entire southern and western boundary, which creates a wedge of land between the river and Tennessee that reaches past the rest of the Alabama and Mississippi border.

The county covers 721 square miles, of which 53 square miles are water. Alabama's legislature established it on February 6, 1818, a year before statehood, and named it for Colonel James Lauderdale of Tennessee. It is part of the Florence-Muscle Shoals metro area, known locally as the Shoals.

Which towns and communities are in Lauderdale County?

Florence is the only city. The towns are Anderson, Killen, Lexington, Rogersville, St. Florian and Waterloo, and Underwood-Petersville is a census-designated place.

Smaller unincorporated communities include Center Star, Elgin, Green Hill, Rhodesville, Zip City, Cloverdale and Mars Hill. Rogersville lies about 23 miles east of Florence, and St. Florian was founded in 1872 by Catholic settlers of German descent. About 52 percent of residents live in rural areas, so many sellers here are dealing with acreage rather than city lots.

A house outside the Florence city limits is served by the Lauderdale County School District. Florence itself has its own city school system, Florence City Schools.

What is the history behind Florence and the county seat?

Florence was established on March 12, 1818 by the Cypress Land Company, which bought 5,515 acres. An Italian engineer, Ferdinand Sannoner, surveyed the town, and he named it after Florence in Tuscany. The site sits on a plateau above the river, which the planners chose in part for protection from flooding.

The University of North Alabama traces its start to LaGrange College, chartered in 1830, and is the state's oldest state-certified university. The Florence Indian Mound, built between 400 BCE and 100 BCE, is the largest surviving earthen mound in Alabama. W. C. Handy was born in a log cabin in Florence in 1873, and the Rosenbaum House, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright in 1939, is the only Wright building in the state.

Historic districts and landmarks can add rules about exterior changes, so ask the city before you plan work on an older downtown house.

What is the economy of Lauderdale County?

Florence is described as northwest Alabama's main economic hub, anchored by the university, the river and the Shoals cities of Muscle Shoals, Sheffield and Tuscumbia just across the water in Colbert County. Together the four cities had 148,779 residents in 2020.

The Port of Florence on Pickwick Lake and the Tennessee Southern Railroad serve local industry. Tourism adds to the mix, with the W. C. Handy Music Festival in summer and the Alabama Renaissance Faire in October. The 2023 American Community Survey puts median household income in Florence at $50,396.

How do the climate and river affect a Lauderdale County house?

Florence has a humid subtropical climate with an average temperature of 59 degrees and 57.06 inches of precipitation a year. Snow averages 2.25 inches a year, which is more than the Alabama average.

  • Spring and fall storms are the main wind risk, and tornadoes damaged the old railroad bridge in 1850 and 1854.
  • A flood washed away the first railroad bridge across the Tennessee River in the 1830s.
  • Low parcels near the river, Elk River or Pickwick Lake deserve a flood check before listing.
  • About half of county residents live in rural areas, where older outbuildings and land drainage also affect value.

Flood or storm damage is hard to hide, and an as-is sale lets an owner skip repairs before closing.

What roads and transit serve Lauderdale County?

U.S. Highways 43 and 72 are the main routes and run together through Florence. The county also has State Routes 17, 20, 64, 99, 101, 133, 157 and 207, plus the Natchez Trace Parkway.

The Shoals do not have a direct interstate link. Florence has no fixed-route bus service, and the Northwest Alabama Council of Local Governments runs a dial-a-ride service. The Northwest Alabama Regional Airport in Muscle Shoals offers service to Charlotte, and Huntsville International is about an hour away.

Florence sits about 70 miles west of Huntsville and about 115 miles northwest of Birmingham, which is a relevant distance for sellers who commute or relocate to those job centers.

Who handles Lauderdale County property tax, and when is it due?

The Lauderdale County Revenue Commissioner assesses property and collects the tax. Taxes are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31, and the office's schedule says unpaid parcels are advertised in April and sold in May.

Ways to pay, from the county FAQ:

  • In person with cash, check, money order or credit card at the Revenue Commissioner's office.
  • By mail.
  • Online at alproptax.com.
  • Credit card use, in person or online, adds a 2.50 percent service fee.

If you have a mortgage, check whether the lender pays the tax from escrow before you send a second payment.

How does Alabama classify property in Lauderdale County?

The county explains three classes. Class I covers utilities at 30 percent, Class II is all other property at 20 percent, and Class III covers agricultural, timber and owner-occupied single-family property at 10 percent. Multiply the appraised value by the class percentage to get assessed value.

The homestead exemption applies to a single-family home you own and live in on the first day of the tax year. The county lists four types:

  • H1, the regular exemption, is $4,000 of assessed value for state tax and $3,000 for county tax.
  • H2 is for owners over 65 with adjusted gross income of $12,000 or less.
  • H3 is for owners who are totally disabled, or over 65 with taxable income under $12,000.
  • H4 is for owners over 65 regardless of income.

Apply before December 31. For an over 65 exemption, bring a driver's license or birth certificate and your latest federal return, and call (256) 760-5785 with questions.

What should a Lauderdale County buyer or seller do about the tax at a sale?

The county gives new owners four steps: record the deed in probate court, assess the property into your name at the Revenue Commissioner's office, claim exemptions or current use status, and finish all of it by December 31 for a purchase made before October 1.

The notice will not show the new owner for that year. The state keeps the name and exemptions on record the previous October 1, so the buyer still has to confirm the tax is paid. Owners who add or remove improvements must report them by December 31 as well.

A manufactured home that is not rented or leased must be assessed at the Revenue Commissioner's office, and the county asks for a bill of sale, a title 20 years old or newer and proof that sales tax was paid. Sellers of mobile homes should gather those papers before listing.

What do Lauderdale County sellers usually face?

  • Rural acreage with a house in poor shape and an unclear boundary.
  • Inherited family land with several heirs.
  • Manufactured homes with title or assessment gaps.
  • Delinquent tax moving toward the May sale.
  • Owners who moved to Huntsville, Birmingham or Tennessee and want to sell without managing repairs from a distance.

Taxes are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31. The Revenue Commissioner's schedule has parcels advertised in April and sold in May.

Is there a fee to pay Lauderdale County tax by credit card?

Yes. Paying by credit card in person or online adds a 2.50 percent service fee, according to the county FAQ.

Record your deed in probate court, assess the property into your name at the Revenue Commissioner's office and claim any exemptions. Finish by December 31 for property bought before October 1.

Elmore County by the numbers

Where is Elmore County, Alabama, and what is its terrain?

Elmore County lies in east central Alabama, just north of Montgomery, and belongs to the Montgomery metropolitan area. Wetumpka is the county seat, and Millbrook is the largest city.

Wikipedia puts the total area at 657 square miles, of which 39 square miles (5.9 percent) is water. The county sits on the fall line, where the Piedmont hills meet the coastal plain, so the land runs from rolling hills to open farm fields. Wetumpka and Tallassee are both river cities on that line.

Coosa, Tallapoosa, Macon, Montgomery, Autauga and Chilton counties surround it. Water frontage, hills and open farmland all appear in the county, so a house description should say what kind of lot comes with it.

What is the history behind Elmore County?

Alabama created Elmore County on February 15, 1866, from parts of Autauga, Coosa, Tallapoosa and Montgomery counties. It was named for General John A. Elmore.

The area's history is older than the county. The French built Fort Toulouse at the junction of the Coosa and Tallapoosa rivers in 1717, and Andrew Jackson built Fort Jackson on the same site in 1814 after the Battle of Horseshoe Bend. Wetumpka formed a city planning board in 1950.

How fast is Elmore County growing?

Wikipedia calls Elmore County one of Alabama's fastest-growing counties. Its population rose from 49,210 in 1990 to 65,874 in 2000, 79,303 in 2010 and 87,977 in 2020, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 91,577.

Who lives in Elmore County and how are homes occupied?

The 2020 census counted 32,567 households in Elmore County, and 31.9 percent had children under 18. About 24.9 percent of households were one person living alone.

The median age was 40.7 years, with 16.7 percent of residents aged 65 or older. Of occupied homes, 24.0 percent were rented. The homeowner vacancy rate was 1.5 percent and the rental vacancy rate was 6.5 percent.

Racial makeup in 2020 was 71.8 percent White and 20.7 percent Black or African American, with 3.2 percent Hispanic or Latino of any race. The county's population grew 10.9 percent from 2010 to 2020.

Which cities and towns are in Elmore County?

Elmore County has four cities and four towns, plus several census-designated places.

  • Cities: Prattville (partly in Autauga County), Millbrook (partly in Autauga County), Tallassee (partly in Tallapoosa County) and Wetumpka.
  • Towns: Coosada, Deatsville, Eclectic and Elmore.
  • Census-designated places: Blue Ridge, Emerald Mountain, Holtville and Redland.

Several of these places cross a county line, which affects where a deed is recorded and who bills the tax. A parcel in the Autauga part of Prattville or Millbrook belongs to a different county than one in Elmore's part.

What drives the Elmore County economy?

The county moved from an agricultural economy to a fast-growing one over the last two decades, according to Wikipedia. Manufacturing is the largest employer sector there.

The state also runs the Julia Tutwiler Prison for Women in Wetumpka, which holds the female death row. Wikipedia cites 1,110 jobs created over four years, though that comes from an older report and carries no date.

What highways serve Elmore County?

Interstate 65 is the main route, and U.S. 82 and U.S. 231 cross the county as well, per Wikipedia.

  • State Route 14 and State Route 9 reach the river towns.
  • State Routes 63, 111, 143, 170, 212 and 229 connect smaller communities.
  • Montgomery County borders Elmore to the south.

Which school systems cover Elmore County homes?

The Elmore County Public School System serves most of the county, and a portion falls in the Tallassee City School District.

A buyer will ask which system covers an address, so a seller should confirm it before listing or accepting an offer. The Census Bureau publishes a school district reference map for the county.

How is property tax run in Elmore County?

Elmore County voters approved a single Revenue Commissioner on March 6, 1990, under Act No. 90-254. That office combined the jobs of tax assessor and tax collector.

The county site says the Revenue Commissioner's office covers about 44,000 parcels over roughly 630 square miles, and also values business personal property and personal aircraft. The office is at 100 E. Commerce Street, Suite 102, in Wetumpka, open Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Its phone is 334-567-1184, and a Citizen Access Portal and a parcel viewer are linked from the county page.

Since July 1, 2020, the same office also handles driver licenses, though that does not affect a property sale.

When are Elmore County property taxes due and what are the penalties?

The October 1 due date and December 31 delinquency date apply, per the Alabama Department of Revenue. Unpaid taxes then follow the statewide sequence to a probate court sale.

  • October 1: tax due
  • January 1: delinquent
  • February: turned over to the Probate Court
  • March: Probate Court meets
  • April: advertised for sale
  • May: tax sale

Etowah County's FAQ states that Alabama law requires interest and penalty at 12 percent a year on past-due taxes, and that a property owner may redeem within 3 years of a sale. Elmore sellers should confirm the exact charge with their own Revenue Commissioner.

What is the fire fee in Elmore County?

Wikipedia notes that voters in the late 1990s passed a mandatory fire fee for volunteer fire services. Every citizen pays the same amount, regardless of the value of the property or income.

Because the amount ignores property value, it stays the same however a house is assessed. A seller should ask the county how the fee is billed.

What does recording a deed cost in Elmore County?

The state's recording privilege tax is fifty cents per $500 of value (Alabama Code 40-22-1). A $250,000 sale equals 500 units of $500, so the tax is $250 before the probate recording fee.

Of the tax collected, two-thirds goes to the state treasury and one-third to the county treasury. A deed without price proof can be taxed on the latest assessment and draw a penalty of $100 or 25 percent of the tax, whichever is greater.

The sale price must be certified on the Department of Revenue form. Etowah County advises buyers to record the deed with the probate office and then assess the property with the Revenue Commissioner, bringing the deed to that office.

What do sellers in Elmore County usually face?

Sellers here range from long-time river-town owners to commuters in newer subdivisions.

  • Inherited houses in Wetumpka or Tallassee with no one living in them
  • Rentals in a fast-growing market where a tenant moved out
  • Houses on or near the river with deferred repairs
  • Owners behind on tax approaching the May sale

The Elmore County Revenue Commissioner, whose office combines assessing and collecting. It is at 100 E. Commerce Street, Suite 102, Wetumpka, phone 334-567-1184.

October 1. They become delinquent after December 31, according to the Alabama Department of Revenue.

Wetumpka. Millbrook is the largest city, per Wikipedia.

Fifty cents for each $500 of value under Alabama Code 40-22-1, so $250 on a $250,000 sale, plus the probate recording fee.

Limestone County by the numbers

Where is Limestone County, Alabama, and how is it laid out?

Limestone County is in the far north of Alabama on the Tennessee line, with Athens as the county seat and the largest city that lies entirely inside the county. The territorial legislature established it on February 6, 1818, and it takes its name from Limestone Creek.

It covers 607 square miles, of which 560 are land and 47 are water, making it the third smallest Alabama county by land area. The Tennessee River and the Elk River both run through it, and part of the Wheeler National Wildlife Refuge lies inside the county. Neighbors include Giles and Lincoln counties in Tennessee, Madison County to the east, and Morgan, Lawrence and Lauderdale counties to the south and west.

The county is part of the Huntsville metropolitan area, so Huntsville-area prices and jobs influence what happens here.

How fast is Limestone County growing?

Which cities, towns and schools make up Limestone County?

Athens, with 25,406 residents in 2020, is the largest city entirely inside the county. The city of Madison is second in population and Huntsville is third, though both are mostly in Madison County. Decatur also touches the county, although it lies mostly in Morgan County.

The incorporated towns are Ardmore, Elkmont, Lester and Mooresville, and Mooresville is the smallest with 47 people in 2020. Unincorporated communities include Belle Mina, Capshaw, Tanner, Veto and Greenbrier.

Five public school systems serve the county:

  • Limestone County Schools, for most areas outside the cities.
  • Athens City Schools.
  • Decatur City Schools.
  • Huntsville City Schools.
  • Madison City Schools.

Higher education in the area includes Athens State University and Calhoun Community College, whose campus is in the southern part of the county near Decatur.

How do roads and airports affect a Limestone County sale?

Limestone County is crossed by Interstate 65, Interstate 565, U.S. 31 and U.S. 72, along with state routes 20, 53, 99, 127 and 251. Freight rail runs on a CSX north-south line and a Norfolk Southern east-west line.

Huntsville International Airport is the closest major commercial airport, about 23 miles east of the county. Nashville is roughly 104 miles to the north.

Where a house sits relative to those highways is one of the facts a buyer will weigh, so mention the nearest interchange when you describe a property.

When are Limestone County property taxes due?

Property taxes in Limestone County follow the state calendar: due October 1 and delinquent after the end of the year. The Alabama Department of Revenue summarizes the full sequence, which runs from the October 1 due date through delinquency on January 1, a turnover to probate court in February, newspaper advertising in April and the tax sale in May.

The county's Revenue Commissioner runs a Citizen Access Portal at limestonerevenue.net, which the office describes as a place to look up real estate and business personal property information. Use it to see the parcel number, owner and bill before you call the office about a payoff.

A tax bill in Alabama combines state, county, municipal and school district levies, so a home inside Athens and a home in the unincorporated county are not billed the same way. Always check the exact parcel instead of comparing two neighbors by price alone.

What can reduce a Limestone County tax bill?

The homestead exemption is the main one, and it applies to a single-family owner-occupied home on up to 160 acres that is your primary residence on the first day of the tax year. You apply at the county office.

  • Homeowners under 65 can receive up to $4,000 of assessed value off the state tax and, in the standard case, $2,000 off the county tax.
  • Owners 65 and older with a low income can qualify for broader relief, and a permanently and totally disabled owner can qualify at any age.
  • Blind owners can qualify at any age for state-level relief.

The exemptions are tied to the person who lives in the house. Sellers should not assume a buyer inherits yours, and heirs who keep a house need to file their own claim.

How do I appeal a Limestone County property assessment?

Start with the county Board of Equalization, the body Alabama law uses to hear value disputes. Ask the Revenue Commissioner's office for the filing window each year, because it follows the date the county announces new values.

If the board does not change the value, section 40-3-25 of the Code of Alabama sets the next step. The appeal to circuit court has to be taken within 30 days of the board's final decision, with notice to the board secretary and the circuit clerk and a bond for costs. A jury can be requested within 10 days, and the loser may appeal to the Alabama Supreme Court within 42 days of the circuit judgment.

Limestone County makes up the 39th Judicial Circuit, which has two circuit judges and two district judges. The court also requires that the earlier year's tax be paid on time, or covered by a bond, for the appeal to proceed.

What happens after a Limestone County tax sale?

The buyer at a tax sale does not take final title right away, because Alabama gives the owner a chance to redeem. Under section 40-10-120, the owner, heirs, personal representatives, a mortgagee or anyone with a legal or equitable interest can redeem within three years of the sale.

A recorded mortgage holder gets an additional year from the date of a written notice from the purchaser. A minor or an incapacitated person has up to one year after the disability is removed. The statute also lets someone redeem part of the land sold.

  • If you own a house that was sold at tax sale, the three-year window is your main deadline.
  • If you inherited the home, heirs are named in the statute as people who can redeem.
  • If you plan to sell, the buyer has to deal with the open tax sale at closing.

What do sellers in Limestone County usually deal with?

The most common situations are inherited houses, rural acreage with an older home, and rentals that an owner no longer wants to manage. About half of the county's residents live in rural areas, so a house here may come with acreage and a longer drive to town, and those details shape what a buyer will pay.

Parts of the county sit along the Elk and Tennessee rivers, and a lender may ask extra questions about a property in that kind of setting. A cash purchase avoids that step.

The Limestone Revenue portal, the probate office and the title company each hold a piece of the file. We gather those pieces so you do not have to chase each office.

The county seat is Athens. Property tax matters go through the Limestone County Revenue Commissioner, which also runs a public portal at limestonerevenue.net.

When are Limestone County property taxes due?

October 1 under the Alabama calendar, and they turn delinquent after the end of the year.

How long can I redeem a Limestone County house after a tax sale?

Three years from the date of sale in most cases, under section 40-10-120 of the Code of Alabama. Some lienholders and people with a legal disability get additional time.

What is the deadline to appeal to circuit court?

30 days after the Board of Equalization's final decision, under section 40-3-25. The taxes must also be paid or bonded to keep the appeal alive.

Yes. The unpaid balance is paid from the closing proceeds, so ask the Revenue Commissioner for a current payoff before you agree to a price.

Madison County by the numbers

Where is Madison County, Alabama, and what is it known for?

Madison County sits in the north central part of Alabama, and Huntsville is both its county seat and its largest city. It was created on December 13, 1808, by the governor of the Mississippi Territory, and it is named for James Madison.

The county covers 813 square miles, of which 802 are land. Much of the modern economy traces to Redstone Arsenal. The Army set it up during World War II, and in 1950 a group of rocket scientists led by Wernher von Braun moved there to develop new rockets. How many people and homes does Madison County have?

The 2020 census counted 388,153 people in Madison County, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 433,516. Only Jefferson County, home to Birmingham, has more residents in Alabama.

Population388,153

Those numbers matter to a seller because one in three occupied homes is rented. Plenty of Madison County houses change hands with a tenant already inside, and that affects how you plan a sale and the closing date.

Which towns and school systems are inside Madison County?

The county contains the cities of Huntsville, Madison, New Hope and Owens Cross Roads, plus the towns of Gurley and Triana. Several larger communities, among them Harvest, Hazel Green, Meridianville, Moores Mill, New Market and Redstone Arsenal, are census-designated places with no city government of their own.

Three public school systems cover the county:

  • Madison County Schools, which serves unincorporated areas plus Gurley, New Hope and Owens Cross Roads, and has high schools in New Market, Hazel Green, Gurley, New Hope and Harvest.
  • Huntsville City Schools, which covers the great majority of Huntsville.
  • Madison City Schools, which also includes the town of Triana.

Why list them on a tax page? Because the address on your deed decides which city, if any, adds its own levy to your bill, and the school system is part of how buyers judge your street.

When are Madison County property taxes due, and when do they go delinquent?

Madison County property taxes are due on October 1 and become delinquent after December 31. The Alabama Department of Revenue lays out the same yearly rhythm: due October 1, delinquent January 1, turned over to probate court in February, advertised in April, and sold at tax sale in May.

The county tax collector explains a few details that surprise new owners:

  • Alabama law does not require a bill to be mailed before the taxes go delinquent. The office sends a courtesy notice by October 1, but a missing notice does not excuse a missed payment.
  • The bill is based on the owner of record on October 1 of the previous year, which is why a former owner can still receive one.
  • Bills cover the period from the previous October 1 through September 30 of the current year.
  • After December 31 there is a $5.00 late fee, interest of 1% per month on the base amount, and probate and advertising fees on top.

The annual tax lien sale is held in May and runs online only. If you plan to sell a house in Madison County during the winter, look at the unpaid year before you list, because the payoff grows every month after the first of the year.

What are the tax rates in Madison County?

The tax collector's FAQ lists the rate per $100 of assessed value by location, and the spread between a Huntsville address and a rural one is wide. These figures come from the county page and can change when the rates are reset, so confirm them with the office.

LocationRate per $100 assessed
Huntsville$5.80
Madison$6.95
Triana$6.15
Gurley, New Hope, Owens Cross Roads$4.05
Unincorporated, land$3.35
Unincorporated, improvements$3.65

The county explains the math this way: appraised value is multiplied by the property classification to get assessed value, the rate is applied, and exemptions are subtracted. A buyer weighing a Madison house against a Huntsville house will see a real difference in the yearly bill for the same price.

How do I appeal a Madison County property value?

You appeal in writing to the Madison County Board of Equalization, which meets at the Madison County Service Center, 2nd Floor, 1918 Memorial Parkway NW, Huntsville. The county cites Code of Alabama sections 40-3-20, 40-3-24 and 40-3-25 for the process.

New values are set each year, usually in March or April, and the county announces them by legal advertisement in the newspaper for two consecutive weeks. You have 30 days from the date of the second advertisement to file. After you file, a county appraiser contacts you to review the value, and if you still disagree a hearing is set before the board.

If the board rules against you, the next step is circuit court. Under section 40-3-25, that appeal must be taken within 30 days of the board's final decision, with notice filed with the board secretary and the circuit clerk. A jury trial can be demanded within 10 days after the appeal is taken, and a further appeal goes to the Alabama Supreme Court within 42 days of the circuit judgment.

One rule trips people up. To keep the circuit court appeal alive, you pay the taxes by December 31, or you post a bond in double the amount of taxes due. Selling the house mid-appeal means settling that question with your closing attorney first.

Which homestead exemptions can reduce a Madison County bill?

Alabama grants a homestead exemption on a single-family home you own and occupy as your primary residence on the first day of the tax year, up to 160 acres. You apply at the county office, not with the state.

  • Owners under 65 get the standard exemption, up to $4,000 of assessed value on the state portion and, in the typical case, $2,000 on the county portion.
  • Owners 65 and older can qualify for larger relief depending on income, and the state's types H-2, H-3 and H-4 spell out the income lines.
  • Owners who are permanently and totally disabled qualify regardless of age, and blind owners qualify for state-level relief.

The Madison County collector shows the formula: with the regular exemption, a bill with assessed value of $4,000 or more is reduced by $48 in state and county taxes. If you bought recently, the collector advises checking that the deed is recorded at the probate office, the property is assessed at the Tax Assessor's office, and your exemption is claimed. Closing attorneys usually handle it, but the county says the owner is ultimately responsible.

Where and how do I pay Madison County property tax?

You can pay online, by mail, or in person at the Madison County Service Center or the Madison satellite office at 100 Plaza Blvd. Both offices are open Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the main number is 256-532-3370.

  • Cards carry a 2.75% convenience fee plus $0.30 per transaction, and the county says none of that fee goes to the county.
  • E-check adds $1.50.
  • Money orders are no longer accepted.
  • In April and May, real property payments must be certified funds, cash, debit or credit card, and personal checks are not taken.
  • Mailed payments must be postmarked by December 31 to avoid the late fee and interest.

Checks are made out to the Madison County Tax Collector. If you did not get a bill, email mctaxcoll@madisoncountyal.gov or call the office, since the exact amount after December 31 changes with fees and interest.

What does Madison County property tax mean when you sell a house?

When you sell, the title company or closing attorney finds the unpaid taxes and subtracts them from your proceeds. Alabama taxes are billed in arrears, so the year that comes due next October 1 is still accruing while you own the house.

These situations come up often on Madison County sales:

  • You are behind on a prior year, and the bill now carries interest, a late fee and advertising costs.
  • The house was inherited and the tax bill is still in a deceased parent's name.
  • A tenant lives in the home, and you want a closing date that fits the lease.
  • The property is already on the delinquent list ahead of the May lien sale.

A cash buyer can close around those problems and pay the county from the proceeds at closing, so you do not have to bring cash to the table. The simplest first step is a phone call to the collector for an exact payoff figure.

More questions about Madison County, AL Property Tax Guide

What is the due date for Madison County, AL property taxes?

October 1. They become delinquent after December 31, and a $5.00 late fee plus 1% monthly interest then applies to the base amount.

Where do I file a property value appeal in Madison County?

With the Madison County Board of Equalization at the Madison County Service Center, 1918 Memorial Parkway NW, Huntsville. You have 30 days from the second newspaper advertisement of new values.

Does Madison County mail a tax bill?

The tax collector sends a courtesy notice by October 1, but Alabama law does not require a bill before delinquency. If you did not receive one, you can look it up online or call 256-532-3370.

What happens if I do not pay Madison County property tax?

The delinquent amount grows with interest and fees, and unpaid parcels can go to the annual online tax lien sale held in May.

Can I sell my Madison County house if taxes are overdue?

Yes. The overdue amount is paid out of the sale proceeds at closing, so ask the collector for an exact payoff before you set a price.

Marshall County by the numbers

Where is Marshall County, Alabama, and what is it like?

Marshall County sits in northeast Alabama along the Tennessee River, with Guntersville as the county seat and Albertville as the largest city. The county was established on January 9, 1836, and covers 623 square miles, of which 57 square miles are water.

The Tennessee River runs both north and south through the county, which gives Marshall County a lake-and-ridge landscape that most inland Alabama counties lack. Lake Guntersville State Park, Cathedral Caverns State Park and Buck's Pocket State Park are all here. Huntsville lies just to the northwest, and Marshall County is part of the Huntsville-Decatur-Albertville combined statistical area.

If you own a house here and owe back property tax, the local map matters. A lake-view house near Guntersville and a rural house in the Sand Mountain area can carry very different tax bills.

Marshall County factFigure
County establishedJanuary 9, 1836
Total area623 square miles (566 land, 57 water)
Population, 2020 census97,612
Housing units, 2020 census41,245, with 9.7% vacant
Owner-occupied share of occupied homes70.5%
Separate parcels appraised by the countyabout 64,000

Which cities and towns are in Marshall County?

Marshall County has four cities of its own, Albertville, Arab, Boaz and Guntersville, plus the towns of Cherokee Ridge, Douglas, Grant and Union Grove. Parts of Arab, Boaz and the Joppa area spill into neighboring counties, and a small piece of Huntsville reaches into Marshall County too.

That patchwork matters for a tax bill. Your total comes from the state, the county, a school district and sometimes a city, and the mix changes depending on which side of a municipal line the house sits on.

  • Albertville: the largest city and home to the county's second courthouse.
  • Guntersville: the county seat, on the lake, with the main courthouse.
  • Arab and Boaz: both partly in a neighboring county, so check which county bills the parcel.
  • Grant, Douglas, Union Grove and Cherokee Ridge: smaller towns where rural parcels dominate.

The county also has many unincorporated communities, among them Asbury, Claysville, Horton and Warrenton, where parcels are usually rural.

Who bills property tax in Marshall County?

The Marshall County Revenue Commissioner assesses and collects property tax, and the office is on the first floor of the Marshall County Courthouse. The Revenue Commissioner sets value at fair and reasonable market value, as if the house sold between a willing buyer and a willing seller.

Alabama taxes property by class. The county's own page lists the classes this way: utilities at 30%, other property at 20%, farm and owner-occupied residential property at 10%, and motor vehicles at 15%. You multiply appraised value by the class percentage to get assessed value, subtract exemptions, and apply the millage rate. A mill is one-tenth of one cent.

Property classAssessment percentage
Class I, utility30%
Class II, all other property20%
Class III, farm and owner-occupied residential10%
Class IV, motor vehicles15%

The county page lists state millage totaling 6.5 mills and county millage totaling 13.5 mills, with school district and city levies added on top. Verify the current figures with the office before you plan around them, because millage can be changed.

Read the Revenue Commissioner's page for the full schedule.

When is property tax due in Marshall County, and what happens if it is late?

Marshall County property tax is due October 1 and becomes delinquent after December 31. The Alabama Department of Revenue states the same dates for the whole state.

The state's published timetable continues from there: the delinquent list goes to probate court in February, the court meets in March, properties are advertised in April, and a tax sale follows in May. A house that falls behind in one year can therefore be on a sale list within about five months of the delinquency date.

  • October 1: taxes due.
  • January 1: taxes delinquent.
  • February: turned over to the probate court.
  • April: advertised for sale.
  • May: tax sale.

You can pay by mail to the Revenue Commissioner, in person at the courthouse, or through a mortgage escrow account. Sellers carrying an unpaid bill should ask for the payoff before listing anything, since a title company will want the figure at closing.

What exemptions apply to a Marshall County home?

The county lists several homestead exemptions, and the first applies to owner-occupied homes where the owner is under 65. Homestead Exemption I is $4,000 against the state tax and $2,000 against county taxes.

Homestead Exemption II covers owners over 65, or blind or totally disabled owners, whose adjusted gross income is under $12,000 a year. It removes all state tax and county tax on up to $5,000 of assessed value. A third exemption exists for owners over 65 or blind or totally disabled.

Current use valuation is a separate tool for Class III property. When the land qualifies, it is taxed on its value to the owner and ignores development potential. Heirs who inherit a house with acreage should ask the office whether current use is in place before they sell.

How do you appeal a Marshall County assessment?

Property owners challenge a value through the county Board of Equalization, and any appeal from the board's ruling must be filed within 30 days of the board's final decision. The statute, Alabama Code 40-3-25, requires notice to the board secretary and to the circuit court clerk, along with a bond.

The same section says an appealing taxpayer has to pay the prior year's taxes before they become delinquent or the appeal can be dismissed, unless a supersedeas bond is posted. That is easy to miss. Someone appealing a high value on a house they plan to sell should not stop paying the bill while the appeal runs.

The Revenue Commissioner is the first office to call. Each parcel has a property record card listing its land and buildings, so ask to see yours and check it against what is actually on the lot.

The statute text is on Justia (2022 edition).

What do buyers and sellers need to do at a Marshall County closing?

Taxes follow the owner, and the county tells new owners to pay by December 31 even when the bill still carries the previous owner's name. The page also tells buyers to confirm the deed is recorded in the probate office and then to assess the property in their own name.

On the recording side, Alabama charges a deed tax of $0.50 for each $500 of value, as set out in Alabama Code 40-22-1. A $150,000 sale therefore carries a $150 deed tax under that rate. A form attesting the real sale price goes with the deed, and the tax is split two thirds to the state and one third to the county.

  • Ask the Revenue Commissioner for the current balance before listing.
  • Confirm whether a homestead or current use status is on the parcel.
  • Expect the title company to pay any unpaid tax from your proceeds.
  • Make sure the deed gets recorded at the probate office after closing.

A cash sale shortens this list because there is no lender waiting on an appraisal or a repair request. The title work still has to be clean.

What do Marshall County sellers usually face?

Sellers in Marshall County often deal with inherited houses or homes that need work. About 29.5% of occupied homes in the county are renter-occupied, so some owners also sell rentals with tenants in place.

Heirs have a particular problem. A house can sit for a year while the estate is opened, and the tax bill keeps arriving in the dead owner's name. If it goes past December 31, interest and the probate court timetable start to apply.

Marshall County also has two courthouses, one in Guntersville and a second in Albertville, so call ahead to confirm where your task is handled.

It depends on the assessed value, exemptions and which city and school district the house is in. The county lists state millage of 6.5 mills and county millage of 13.5 mills, and school and city levies are added to those.

When is Marshall County property tax due?

October 1, with delinquency after December 31. The Revenue Commissioner collects it at the courthouse, by mail, or through a mortgage escrow account.

Who do I call about a Marshall County assessment?

The Marshall County Revenue Commissioner, whose office is on the first floor of the courthouse. That office values property, assesses new owners and answers exemption questions.

Can I sell a Marshall County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The unpaid amount is normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing, so ask the Revenue Commissioner for a payoff figure before you accept an offer.

What is the Alabama deed tax?

Alabama Code 40-22-1 sets the deed tax at $0.50 for each $500 of value. A form stating the actual purchase price must accompany the deed.

What should a Jefferson County homeowner know about the county itself?

Jefferson County is the most populous county in Alabama and the central county of the Birmingham-Hoover metro area. It had 674,721 residents in 2020, and the Census estimate for 2025 is 665,742.

The county stretches over roughly 1,124 square miles of ridge and valley country, which makes it the fifth largest in Alabama by land area. It was established in 1819, and its first seats were Carrollsville and then Elyton, which served until 1873. The county's long history of iron, coal and limestone mining and steelmaking explains why so many neighborhoods began as company or industrial towns.

Which cities and areas make up Jefferson County?

The county holds dozens of municipalities and unincorporated communities. The larger cities include Birmingham, Bessemer, Hoover, Homewood, Vestavia Hills, Mountain Brook, Trussville, Gardendale, Hueytown, Pleasant Grove, Center Point and Fultondale.

Some of them straddle county lines. Birmingham, Hoover, Vestavia Hills, Helena, Leeds and Trussville each reach partly into another county, and Sumiton and Warrior do the same. If your house is in one of those places, the county that bills the tax depends on where the parcel sits, not on the city name in the mailing address.

Several former towns, including Ensley, North Birmingham, Woodlawn and Elyton, are now Birmingham neighborhoods. Their housing stock is often older, and long-owned family homes there change hands through estates more often than newer subdivisions do.

What are the Jefferson County property tax dates?

The Alabama Department of Revenue states that property taxes are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31. That schedule applies in Jefferson County as it does across the state.

The state timetable that follows runs like this:

  • October 1: taxes due.
  • January 1: taxes delinquent.
  • February: delinquent accounts turned over to the probate court.
  • March: the probate court meets.
  • April: parcels advertised for sale.
  • May: tax sale.

A bill covers the previous tax year, so a payment made in the fall is for the year that ended the prior September 30, according to how the neighboring Lauderdale County office explains the cycle. If you sell in the middle of the year, the closing agent splits the tax between buyer and seller.

How does Alabama classify and value a Jefferson County house?

Alabama taxes property by class. As published by the Lauderdale County revenue office, Class I is utility property at 30 percent, Class II is all other property at 20 percent, and Class III is agricultural, timber and owner-occupied single-family property at 10 percent.

Appraised value times the class percentage gives assessed value, and the bill is based on assessed value less any exemptions. Because an owner-occupied house sits in the 10 percent class, a rental or second home can carry a heavier assessment than the house next door that is lived in. That difference surprises landlords who sell a Jefferson County rental.

Exemptions generally require an application, and the dollar amounts are set county by county, so confirm yours with the Jefferson County offices before you rely on a number from another county's page.

Who handles Jefferson County property tax questions?

Jefferson County splits the work between a tax assessor, who sets values and hears appeals, and a tax collector, who sends bills and takes payments.

If you do not receive a bill, contact the collector's office. Madison County's published guidance says Alabama law does not require a bill before taxes turn delinquent, so the burden stays with the owner.

The probate court is a separate office. It records the deed after a sale, and it also takes custody of delinquent accounts under the state timetable.

What happens to the tax bill when a Jefferson County house is sold?

The first bill after a sale often shows the previous owner. Lauderdale County explains that the state requires the notice to remain in the name on record the prior October 1, with any exemptions that owner held.

That does not move the responsibility. A buyer owes tax on property they own regardless of whose name is printed on the notice. For sellers, this means two checks at closing:

  • Confirm the current year's tax is paid or prorated.
  • Make sure any delinquent prior-year tax is paid off from the proceeds.
  • Keep a copy of the payoff statement.

Lauderdale's guidance also tells new owners to record the deed, assess the property into their name and claim exemptions before December 31 for purchases made before October 1.

What happens when Jefferson County property tax goes delinquent?

The account moves along the state timetable toward a May sale. Penalties, interest and advertising costs are added along the way, so the amount owed grows each month.

Selling before the sale date is usually the cleaner route. A title company can pay the tax from your proceeds at closing. If the debt is larger than the equity in the house, bring the numbers to the title company early so you know what the closing statement will show.

Does the county's finance history affect homeowners today?

The county declared bankruptcy in 2011 after sewer rates climbed more than 300 percent over 15 years and risky bond swaps led to about $4 billion in debt. Wikipedia describes it as the largest municipal bankruptcy in the country at the time.

The county has limited home rule. It can set zoning, maintain sewers and highways and handle trash disposal, and it can enforce taxation other than property taxes. Property tax rates still come from the statutory process, which is why the same October 1 and December 31 dates apply in Jefferson County as in Lauderdale.

How do roads and rail shape Jefferson County neighborhoods?

Five interstates cross the county: I-20, I-22, I-59, I-65 and I-459, and Wikipedia lists future I-222 and I-422 as well. U.S. Routes 11, 31, 78, 280 and 411 add the older corridors.

Amtrak's Crescent stops in Birmingham, freight rail is run by BNSF, CSX and Norfolk Southern, and Birmingham-Shuttlesworth International Airport handles air service.

What do Jefferson County sellers usually face?

  • Estate sales in older Birmingham neighborhoods with several heirs.
  • Rental houses with a higher tax class and deferred repairs.
  • Houses with delinquent tax moving toward the spring sale.
  • Parcels near a county line where the billing office is not obvious.
  • Owners who live out of state and have not seen a bill.

What property classes does Alabama use?

Class I is utilities at 30 percent, Class II is all other property at 20 percent, and Class III is agricultural, timber and owner-occupied single-family property at 10 percent, as published by Lauderdale County.

Why is my Jefferson County tax bill in the previous owner's name?

Alabama keeps the notice in the name on record the previous October 1. The new owner is still responsible for the tax, so confirm it is paid.

Can I sell a Jefferson County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The tax is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, and the title company gets the payoff figure from the tax office.

How does property tax work in Shelby County, Alabama?

A Shelby County owner pays property tax on an assessed value multiplied by the millage rates of the taxing bodies that cover the parcel. The Alabama Department of Revenue explains a mill as one tenth of one cent and gives a worked example: a $100,000 appraised value at a 10 percent assessment rate becomes a $10,000 assessed value, which at a county rate of 0.0325 produces a $325 bill.

That example uses the state's own illustration, not a Shelby County rate. Your actual bill depends on the millage for your city, school district and any special districts, which the county tax office can give you for your parcel. Two things can raise a bill. A taxing authority can raise the millage, or the appraised value can rise through a court-ordered reappraisal or a market increase. The department's FAQ says all Alabama counties now run annual reappraisal, reviewing one quarter of the county each year, so every parcel is looked at over a four-year cycle.

What are the key tax dates for a Shelby County house?

Alabama taxes are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31. If they go unpaid, the department's timetable runs from delinquency on January 1 to a turnover to the probate court in February, a court meeting in March, advertising in April and a tax sale in May.
