Counties are not required to mail notices. The Revenue Department says the tax bill is a courtesy, and you owe the tax whether or not one arrives.

What changes to a house have to be reported in Shelby County?

Owners must visit the county revenue office by December 31 and sign a new assessment for any improvement or removal made on or before October 1 of that year. The list of reportable items includes new structures and additions, pools, remodeling, an added bath or fireplace, a patio, deck, carport or garage.

Normal upkeep does not count. Re-roofing, minor repairs and painting do not require a reassessment. If you are preparing a Shelby County house for sale, keep a record of any work that fits the first list, because an unreported addition can surface later as a corrected assessment.

  • Reportable: additions, pools, decks, garages, carports, added baths
  • Not reportable: re-roofing, painting, minor repairs
  • Deadline: December 31 for work done by October 1

Does Shelby County offer a homestead exemption?

Yes. Alabama defines a homestead as a single-family, owner-occupied dwelling and its land, up to 160 acres, occupied as the primary residence on the first day of the tax year. Owners over 65, permanently and totally disabled owners, and blind owners are exempt from the state portion, though county taxes may still be due.

You claim an exemption at the local county office. The state page does not list Shelby's own exemption amounts, so ask the county for them. The state ties the exemption to the owner who occupies the home on the first day of the tax year, so a buyer who moves in applies for their own.

What do you do about property tax when you buy or sell in Shelby County?

The state's guidance for a purchase is short: record the deed in the probate office, then assess the property at the county revenue office, and bring the deed. Make sure any taxes for the year are paid, and know that the bill may still carry the previous owner's name. The new owner is responsible for the taxes on property they own whatever name is on the bill.

For a seller, that means the closing statement should say who pays the current year's tax. Tax proration practice is a matter for the contract and the title company, and we did not find a Shelby County rule on it, so settle it in writing. Report any address change to the county office in writing as well.

Appeals follow their own deadlines, and we could not confirm the Shelby County appeal window from an official page. If you think an assessment is wrong, ask the county office how to file and by what date before you list the house.

What if Shelby County taxes are unpaid when I want to sell?

You can still sell, but the timetable keeps running. A bill that is not paid by December 31 turns delinquent on January 1 and moves toward the probate court and a possible May tax sale, so the earlier you find an unpaid balance, the more choices you have.

If a balance is due at closing, the contract and the closing agent can provide for paying it out of the sale proceeds. A sale to a cash buyer can close on a short schedule, which helps when a deadline is close, though we do not promise a closing date before we have seen the title.

  • Ask the county tax office for the payoff on every year that shows a balance.
  • Check whether any improvement was left unreported.
  • Keep proof of any exemption you held in case the office asks.

Where is Shelby County and what are its towns?

Shelby County is in central Alabama, covers 810 square miles and has Columbiana as its seat, according to Wikipedia's county entry. Alabaster is the largest city, and the county had 223,024 residents in 2020 with a 2025 estimate of 238,552.

The county's incorporated places include Alabaster, Calera, Chelsea, Columbiana, Helena, Montevallo, Pelham, Westover, Harpersville, Indian Springs Village, Wilsonville and Wilton. Birmingham, Hoover, Leeds, Vestavia Hills and Vincent have parts inside the county but extend into neighboring ones, so confirm which county's records cover your parcel.

Interstate 65 and U.S. 31 run north to south, and U.S. 231 and U.S. 280 cross the east. Commercial flights use Birmingham-Shuttlesworth International Airport in neighboring Jefferson County, while the Shelby County Airport handles general aviation.

What do Shelby County property owners like to know about the area?

The county has several parks and sites that buyers recognize. Wikipedia lists Oak Mountain State Park, Oak Mountain Amphitheatre, Cahaba River Wildlife Management Area, the Aldrich Coal Mine Museum, the Heart of Dixie Railroad Museum, Shelby Iron Works Park and American Village among its places of interest.

Schools come from four public systems: Shelby County Schools, Alabaster City Schools, Pelham City Schools and Hoover City Schools. Private schools in the county include Briarwood Christian School and Indian Springs School. Which district a house falls into depends on the address, so check with the school systems rather than assuming.

A cash sale does not change the property tax steps. The buyer takes the house as is, taxes are settled at closing as the contract says, and the new owner reports the deed to the probate office.

More questions about Shelby County, AL Property Tax Guide

When are Shelby County property taxes due?

October 1, and they become delinquent after December 31, according to the Alabama Department of Revenue. Unpaid taxes can go to a tax sale the following May.

Do I have to pay if I never got a tax bill?

Yes. The Revenue Department says counties are not required to mail notices and do so as a courtesy, so the tax is owed regardless.

What work on my Shelby County house has to be reported?

New structures, additions, pools, remodeling, added baths or fireplaces, patios, decks, carports and garages. Re-roofing, painting and minor repairs do not need a reassessment. The deadline is December 31 for work done on or before October 1.

Who pays the tax when a Shelby County house sells mid-year?

The state says the new owner answers for taxes on property they own, even if the bill carries the old owner's name. How the year is divided between buyer and seller is set in the sale contract.

How do I appeal a Shelby County assessment?

Chilton County by the numbers

Where is Chilton County, Alabama?

Chilton County lies in central Alabama, south of Shelby County and inside the Birmingham metropolitan area, with Clanton as its seat and largest city. It covers 701 square miles, of which 693 is land and 7.9 is water.

Seven counties border it: Shelby to the north, Coosa to the east, Elmore to the southeast, Autauga to the south, Perry and Dallas to the southwest and Bibb to the northwest. The landscape is varied. The county has swamps, prairies, the foothills of the Appalachians, which end here, and the Coosa River. Part of the Talladega National Forest falls inside the line.

One odd fact for a county this size: in 2010 the center of population of the whole state of Alabama was in Chilton County, near the city of Jemison.

How did Chilton County start, and why is Clanton the seat?

The county was created on December 30, 1868 as Baker County, built from parts of Autauga, Bibb, Perry and Shelby counties, with Grantville as its seat. Residents petitioned for a new name, and on December 17, 1874 they accepted the suggestion of Chilton, after William Parish Chilton Sr., a lawyer who became chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court.

The seat moved in 1871 to the place now called Clanton after the Grantville courthouse burned. Clanton was a stop on the Louisville and Nashville Railroad when it was chosen, and it carries the name of James H. Clanton. If you hold a deed or probate paperwork from the 1800s, expect the county names above to show up in old records.

How fast is Chilton County growing?

Chilton County grew from 43,643 people in 2010 to 45,014 in 2020, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 47,708, a gain of 6.0 percent over the 2020 count. The table shows how the housing stock looked at the 2020 census.

Land here is mostly rural, and three out of four occupied homes are owned by the people living in them. That points to many sales coming from family owners, not investors.

What cities, towns and schools make up Chilton County?

Chilton County has three cities, two towns and a single public school district, the Chilton County School District, serving roughly 7,700 students from pre-K through 12th grade.

  • Cities: Clanton (county seat), Jemison and Calera, which lies mostly in Shelby County.
  • Towns: Maplesville and Thorsby.
  • Unincorporated communities include Isabella, Jumbo, Mountain Creek, Mulberry, Pletcher, Stanton and Verbena.

With one school district, a buyer comparing Clanton and Jemison does not face the district switch that families deal with in Calhoun or Colbert counties. That keeps the county simple to market, though the place you sell in still shapes who looks at your house.

The county is run by a seven-member commission, which hires a county administrator for daily management. Chilton County adopted cumulative voting for commission elections in 1988.

The long-run population line explains a lot about the housing stock. Chilton County had 26,922 people in 1950, dipped to 25,180 in 1970, then climbed to 30,612 in 1980, 32,458 in 1990 and 39,593 in 2000. Houses built in the 1980s and 1990s growth years are now old enough that roofs and mechanical systems may be due for replacement.

What do peaches, highways and weather mean for a Chilton County house?

Chilton County is known for its peaches, and Interstate 65 runs through it, along with U.S. 31, U.S. 82 and a set of state routes including 22, 139, 143, 145, 155, 183 and 191. The Louisville and Nashville Railroad was already at Clanton when the town was picked as the county seat in 1871.

Calera, mostly in Shelby County, sits on the northern edge and ties the county to the Birmingham area. Farther south the land turns to prairie, swamp and river bottom, so two houses a few miles apart can differ a lot in drainage and access.

Older farmhouses and outbuildings are common in a county that is 85.5 percent rural. If an outbuilding was torn down or a room was added years ago, the tax record may still show the old layout. We take houses in that condition without asking for repairs first.

When are Chilton County property taxes due, and what happens if they are late?

Property tax is due October 1 and delinquent after December 31, according to the Alabama Department of Revenue. The state's published timetable has five steps after that.

  • January 1: taxes are delinquent.
  • February: the account is turned over to the probate court.
  • March: the probate court meets.
  • April: the property is advertised for sale.
  • May: the tax sale is held.

Alabama counties are not required to mail a notice, and the Revenue Commissioner sends statements only as a courtesy. A house that sat empty through a probate case can slip into this cycle without the heirs seeing a bill.

What must a Chilton County owner report after changing the house?

An owner or an agent must visit the Revenue Commissioner's office no later than December 31 to sign a new assessment reporting any improvement or removal made on or before October 1 of that year, per the Department of Revenue.

The department lists examples that count: new structures or additions, swimming pools, extensive repairs, remodeling or renovation, and adding a fireplace, an extra bath, a patio, a deck, a carport or a garage. Re-roofing, minor repairs and painting are normal maintenance and do not require a new assessment.

For a seller this matters in both directions. An unreported addition can mean the parcel was assessed too low, and a torn-down barn that still sits on the record can mean you are paying for a building that is gone.

How does a Chilton County appeal work?

You protest in writing to the county Board of Equalization, and Alabama gives you 30 days after you receive written notice of the value. The process is laid out in Code of Alabama sections 40-3-20, 40-3-24 and 40-3-25.

The state also reviews one quarter of each county every year under its annual equalization program, so a parcel can be reassessed on a four-year rotation. Homeowners who are over 65, permanently and totally disabled or blind are exempt from the state portion of the tax, but they must contact the local official to claim the homestead exemption.

What does it cost to record a deed in Chilton County?

The state recordation tax is 50 cents per $500 of value, or part of it, under section 40-22-1 of the Code of Alabama. A $175,000 sale equals 350 units, so the tax is $175, not counting the probate recording fee.

Two-thirds of the tax goes to the state treasury and one-third to the county. The instrument must carry proof of the actual sales price on the Department of Revenue form.

What is the county seat of Chilton County, Alabama?

Clanton is the county seat and the largest city. The seat moved there in 1871 after the Grantville courthouse burned.

When did Chilton County get its name?

Chilton County took its present name on December 17, 1874. It was created in 1868 as Baker County.

Is Chilton County rural?

Yes. The 2020 census counted 85.5 percent of residents as living in rural areas and 14.5 percent in urban areas.

When do Chilton County taxes become delinquent?

They become delinquent after December 31 for the tax year, having come due on October 1. The tax sale follows in May.

Yes. We look at houses in any condition, and we can review the tax account together before you decide whether to accept an offer.

Colbert County by the numbers

Where is Colbert County, Alabama, and what is it known for?

Colbert County is in the northwest corner of Alabama along the Tennessee River, with Tuscumbia as the county seat and Muscle Shoals as the largest city. It is part of the Florence-Muscle Shoals metropolitan area, which locals call the Shoals.

Lauderdale County is to the north, Lawrence County to the southeast, Franklin County to the south and Tishomingo County, Mississippi, to the west. The county covers 622 square miles, and 30 of them are water, nearly 5 percent. Elevation ranges from 410 feet at the river to 980 feet in the southeast.

The Natchez Trace Parkway crosses a piece of the county. So do creeks, springs and ridges with names like Bald Knob, Underwood Mountain and Sand Mountain, which means a house here can sit near a floodplain or up on a slope depending on the street.

How did Colbert County come to exist?

Colbert County was set up on February 6, 1867, split from Franklin County, then abolished eight months later on November 29, 1867 by a constitutional convention. Voters asked for it back, and the legislature restored it on February 24, 1870.

It is named for the brothers George and Levi Colbert, Chickasaw chiefs in the early 1800s. In 1890 the eastern boundary moved from County Line Road to Town Creek, which put the whole town of Leighton inside the county. Deeds that describe land near that line sometimes carry the old reference.

What do the Colbert County numbers look like?

Colbert County had 57,227 residents at the 2020 census, up 5.1 percent from 54,428 in 2010, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 59,474. Here are the housing details from the 2020 count.

Colbert County's population history is steady. It had 31,997 people in 1920, 39,561 in 1950, 54,519 in 1980 and 51,666 in 1990, then 54,984 in 2000 and 54,428 in 2010. Of today's residents, 59.7 percent live in urban areas and 40.3 percent in rural ones.

The median age of 42.6 is a little above the 40 to 41 range in neighboring Alabama counties such as Calhoun, Chilton and Cullman, and 19.9 percent of residents are 65 or older. That age mix is why homestead rules for seniors matter so much here.

Which towns and school systems serve Colbert County?

Colbert County has three cities, three towns and four public school systems, one for each of the main cities plus the county system.

  • Cities: Muscle Shoals, Sheffield and Tuscumbia (county seat).
  • Towns: Cherokee, Leighton and Littleville.
  • School systems: Colbert County Schools, Muscle Shoals City, Sheffield City and Tuscumbia City.
  • College: Northwest Shoals Community College.

Unincorporated communities include Allsboro, Barton, Buzzard Roost, Ford City, Hatton, Listerhill, Maud, Mountain Mills, Nitrate City, Pride, Spring Valley and Village Number 1. School boundaries follow the city or county system, so a buyer should confirm the district for a specific address.

Why do music and Helen Keller matter to Colbert County sellers?

The county's history is part of why people visit. Ivy Green in Tuscumbia is the birthplace of Helen Keller, and the cities of Sheffield and Muscle Shoals are where musicians as different as Aretha Franklin and the Rolling Stones recorded.

The county also has F.A.M.E. Recording Studios in Muscle Shoals, the Alabama Music Hall of Fame in Tuscumbia, Wilson Lock and Dam, the Tennessee Valley Art Museum, the Tuscumbia Railroad Depot Museum and the Nitrate Village Number 1 Historic District in Sheffield.

Annual events listed for the county include the Helen Keller Festival in June, the W.C. Handy Music Festival in July and the Coon Dog Labor Day Celebration in September at the Key-Underwood Coon Dog Memorial Graveyard.

How do roads and rail work in Colbert County?

U.S. 43 and U.S. 72 are the main highways, with State Routes 20, 133, 157, 184 and 247 and the Natchez Trace Parkway also crossing the county. Norfolk Southern runs freight lines south, east and west.

Rivers and parks shape where people want to live. The county lists Rivermont Park on the Tennessee River in Tuscumbia, Colbert Ferry Park in Cherokee, Highland Park and Spring Park in Tuscumbia, John W. Gattman Park in Muscle Shoals, Tenth Avenue Park and York Terrace Park in Sheffield, and the Thomas State Wildlife Refuge at Barton.

Northwest Alabama Regional Airport and Big River Airpark are listed as the county's airports. Sellers near the river or the rail corridor should expect a buyer to ask about noise and flood status.

How does Alabama define a homestead, and who is exempt?

Alabama defines a homestead as a single-family, owner-occupied dwelling and its land, up to 160 acres. To qualify you must own the home and live in it as your primary residence on the first day of the tax year you are applying for.

People over 65, people who are permanently and totally disabled and people who are blind are exempt from the state portion of the property tax, though county taxes may still be due. You claim the exemption at the local tax office. Manufactured home owners over 65 are also exempt from the registration fee on an owner-occupied home, but they still pay the $5 issuance fee.

With about one in five Colbert County residents at 65 or older, many sellers here already hold an exemption. If you sell, tell the tax office, because the next owner has to apply on their own.

How do mills turn into a Colbert County tax bill?

A mill is one-tenth of one cent. The tax is the assessed value times the millage rate, and the assessed value is a percentage of the appraised value.

The Department of Revenue gives this example: a $100,000 appraised value at a 10 percent assessment rate is $10,000 assessed value, and at a county millage of 0.0325 the tax is $325. Your actual rate depends on the county, the city and the school district that cover your parcel.

The Department also lists two reasons a bill goes up:

  • a vote or board decision to raise the millage rate;
  • an increase in the appraised value of the property.

Taxes are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31. If no statement reaches you, the obligation is the same.

Is a deed tax owed when a Colbert County family transfers a house?

Not always. Section 40-22-1 of the Alabama Code exempts deeds executed for a nominal consideration to perfect title to real estate, as well as re-recorded corrected deeds, and it exempts transfers of mortgages on which the mortgage tax was already paid.

Everything else pays 50 cents for each $500 of value, and the recorder must receive proof of the actual price or value. If no proof comes with the deed, the office falls back on the latest assessment and anyone who intentionally withholds proof after a request faces a penalty of $100 or 25 percent of the tax, whichever is greater. For an heir fixing a family title, the nominal-consideration route is worth asking the probate office about before you sign.

Muscle Shoals is the largest city. Tuscumbia is the county seat.

They are exempt from the state portion if they claim the homestead exemption, but county taxes may still be due. File the claim at the local tax office.

What is a mill on an Alabama tax bill?

A mill is one-tenth of one cent, and the bill is the assessed value times the millage rate.

We can. Delinquent taxes after December 31 are normally settled out of the sale proceeds, and we will go over the balance with you before making an offer.

Tuscaloosa County by the numbers

Where is Tuscaloosa County, Alabama, and how large is it?

Tuscaloosa County covers 1,351 square miles in the west-central part of Alabama, a region people call West Alabama. It is the second-largest county in the state by land area and third-largest by total area, with 1,322 square miles of land and 30 of water.

Seven counties border it: Walker to the northeast, Jefferson to the east, Bibb to the southeast, Hale to the south, Greene to the southwest, Pickens to the west and Fayette to the northwest. The county sits on the line between the Appalachian Highlands and the Gulf Coastal Plain, so the land changes from forested hills to flatter ground. Part of the Talladega National Forest lies inside it.

The Black Warrior River cuts through the county, and Lake Tuscaloosa covers about 5,000 acres. Houses near water, hills or the forest edge each carry their own access, flood and insurance questions.

How did Tuscaloosa County begin?

The county was established on February 6, 1818, and the town of Tuskaloosa was incorporated on December 13, 1819, one day before Congress admitted Alabama as a state. The name honors Chief Tuskaloosa, and Wikipedia traces it to two Choctaw words meaning warrior and black.

From 1826 to 1846 the town served as the capital of Alabama. The University of Alabama was established there in 1831. In the 1890s the Army Corps of Engineers built locks and dams on the Black Warrior River that tied the county to the seaport of Mobile by water.

What do the housing numbers look like in Tuscaloosa County?

A rental vacancy rate of 11.6 percent is the figure landlords should watch. A rental house with a hard-to-replace tenant or damage from the last lease can sit a while before it fills again.

What drives the Tuscaloosa County economy?

The University of Alabama is the county's largest employer, and the Mercedes-Benz plant near Vance is the main industrial anchor. Mercedes announced the plant in 1993, opened it in 1995, and the county page says the company employed over 4,000 people there as of 2021.

The county's economic development authority lists the largest employers as the University of Alabama, Mercedes-Benz U.S. International, DCH Regional Medical Center, the county and city boards of education, Warrior Met Coal, the City of Tuscaloosa, Michelin/BF Goodrich, the Veterans Administration Medical Center, SMP Automotive Systems, Phifer, Brose, Northport Medical Center, ARD Logistics, Shelton State Community College, Bryce Hospital, Nucor and ZF Chassis Systems. Education, health care and advanced manufacturing lead that list.

The University of Alabama, Shelton State and Stillman College enrolled 43,681 students combined in spring 2021, which keeps a steady stream of renters and short-term residents in the market.

Which cities, towns and schools make up Tuscaloosa County?

The county has three cities: Tuscaloosa, the county seat and largest city, plus Northport and Brookwood. Six towns are listed: Coaling, Coker, Lake View, Moundville, Vance and Woodstock. Cottondale and Holt are census-designated places.

Two public school systems share the county. Tuscaloosa City Schools serve the city and the Tuscaloosa County School System serves residents outside it. The county system lists Brookwood, Hillcrest, Holt, Northside, Sipsey Valley and Tuscaloosa County High School, and the city system has Paul W. Bryant, Central and Northridge high schools.

What weather and hazards matter for a Tuscaloosa County house?

Tornadoes are the hazard that shaped the county's recent history. On April 27, 2011, an EF4 tornado struck Tuscaloosa, and Wikipedia records more than $1 billion in public and private recovery funding in the decade afterward.

The area has a humid subtropical climate, and Wikipedia notes that severe thunderstorms can bring damaging winds, large hail and occasional tornadoes. If your house had storm repairs, keep the permits and receipts, because a buyer or lender may ask for them.

The Tax Assessor values property and the Tax Collector bills and collects it, both at 714 Greensboro Ave in Tuscaloosa. The collector is in Room 124 at (205) 464-8230, open Monday to Friday 8:30am to 5pm except holidays, and the assessor is in Room 108 at (205) 464-8240.

The appraisal department reviews real estate values on a four-year cycle required by Alabama statute, and appraisers also check yearly changes. The county names building permits, septic permits, recent sales and taxpayer requests as reasons a value gets reviewed.

For 2026, the county posted valuation notices as of May 1, 2026, with a protest deadline of May 31, 2026. The assessor's page lists a protest form, a homestead type chart, income qualifications, a millage chart and a form for disability requirements. We did not extract millage numbers, so check the chart on the county site for the rate in your area.

Because permits are one trigger for a value review, a permitted remodel can lead to a new valuation. Keep that in mind before you spend money on a house you plan to sell.

How do I appeal a Tuscaloosa County value?

You file a written protest with the County Board of Equalization, and Alabama gives you 30 days after written notice of valuation. The Department of Revenue cites Code of Alabama sections 40-3-20, 40-3-24 and 40-3-25.

The county's assessor page links a protest form. Use the deadline printed on your notice, which for 2026 was May 31.

What do Tuscaloosa County sellers run into?

With a median age of 32.9 and 41.1 percent of occupied homes rented, a former rental can carry wear that a family buyer may not accept.

  • Student rentals with deferred repairs after turnover.
  • Storm-damaged roofs and trees in a county with a recent tornado history.
  • Estate houses where heirs live outside the county.
  • Property bills that went to an old mailing address.

A cash sale can close without a lender's repair demands, and the tax balance is settled from the proceeds at closing.

Property taxes are due October 1, and December 31 is the last day to pay without penalties or interest. Taxes turn delinquent on January 1.

The Tax Collector is at 714 Greensboro Ave, Room 124, Tuscaloosa, AL 35401, and can be reached at (205) 464-8230. Hours are Monday to Friday, 8:30am to 5pm, except holidays.

When does the Tuscaloosa County tax sale happen?

The county advertises the impending sale online in April and holds its annual tax sale, online only, in the last week of April.

What was the 2026 protest deadline in Tuscaloosa County?

The county's 2026 valuation notices listed a protest deadline of May 31, 2026, for values estimated as of May 1, 2026.

How often does Tuscaloosa County reappraise property?

The appraisal department says Alabama statutes require it to maintain real estate values and reestablish its county index within a four-year period, and it reviews yearly changes as well.

Can I sell a Tuscaloosa County house with delinquent taxes?

Yes. The closing agent obtains a payoff from the Tax Collector, and the balance is paid from the sale proceeds.

Calhoun County by the numbers

Where is Calhoun County, Alabama, and how big is it?

Calhoun County sits in the east central part of Alabama, with Anniston as the county seat and Oxford as the largest city. The Census Bureau puts the total area at 612 square miles, of which 606 is land and 6.4 is water.

Five counties touch it: Cherokee to the northeast, Cleburne to the east, Talladega to the south, St. Clair to the west and Etowah to the northwest. Part of the Talladega National Forest lies inside the county, and so does the Mountain Longleaf National Wildlife Refuge. Together Anniston and Oxford make up the Anniston-Oxford metropolitan area.

The 2020 census counted 116,441 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 115,834. That is a county that has hovered near the same size for forty years: 119,761 people in 1980, 116,034 in 1990, 112,249 in 2000 and 118,572 in 2010. For a seller, a flat population usually means the buyer pool is made of people already living here, not a wave of newcomers.

How did Calhoun County get its name and its county seat?

The county began on December 18, 1832 as Benton County, with Jacksonville as its seat, and was renamed Calhoun County on January 29, 1858. The new name honors John C. Calhoun, a U.S. senator from South Carolina.

Anniston took over as county seat after years of controversy and a state Supreme Court ruling in June 1900. That is why the courthouse you visit for county business is in Anniston, while Jacksonville, the old seat, is now known mostly for Jacksonville State University, founded in 1883 and enrolling more than 9,000 students.

What are the key numbers for Calhoun County homes?

The 2020 census shows 46,437 households in Calhoun County and 53,052 housing units, which leaves roughly one unit in eight empty. The table below lists the figures we confirmed on the Census Bureau's 2020 data as summarized on Wikipedia.

A rental vacancy rate above 12 percent tells you rental houses can sit empty for a while here. Owners of inherited or tenant-worn rentals feel that sooner than owners of occupied family homes.

Which cities, towns and school systems are in Calhoun County?

Calhoun County has seven cities and two towns, and five public school districts that do not follow the county line.

  • Cities: Anniston, Glencoe (partly in Etowah County), Jacksonville, Oxford (partly in Talladega and Cleburne counties), Piedmont (partly in Cherokee County), Southside (partly in Etowah County) and Weaver.
  • Towns: Hobson City and Ohatchee.
  • Census-designated places: Alexandria, Choccolocco, Nances Creek, Saks, West End-Cobb Town and White Plains.
  • School districts: Anniston City, Calhoun County, Jacksonville City, Oxford City and Piedmont City, with about 17,000 students across the public schools.

Because several cities straddle a county line, a house with an Oxford or Glencoe mailing address may be taxed by a different county than you expect. Check the parcel record before you assume which office bills you.

Higher education is local too: Gadsden State Community College runs a campus in Anniston, and Jacksonville State University is in Jacksonville.

How do roads, rail and weather affect a Calhoun County house?

Interstate 20 is the main road through Calhoun County, joined by U.S. 78, U.S. 278, U.S. 431 and a long list of state routes. Amtrak's Crescent stops here, and Norfolk Southern and the Alabama and Tennessee River Railway run freight lines.

Weather matters to a buyer's inspection. A tornado rated F4 struck the county during the 1994 Palm Sunday outbreak on March 27, 1994 and destroyed Goshen United Methodist Church in Piedmont. A storm like that is the kind of event that leaves roof and structural repairs behind, and those repairs shape what an inspector flags on resale.

For transit, the Areawide Community Transportation System serves the county. Recreation draws buyers too: the Chief Ladiga Trail crosses Calhoun and Cleburne counties, and the Coldwater Covered Bridge and the Anniston Museum of Natural History are local landmarks.

How do I protest my Calhoun County property value?

You file a written protest with the county Board of Equalization within 30 days after you receive written notice of the valuation. The Alabama Department of Revenue points to Code of Alabama sections 40-3-20, 40-3-24 and 40-3-25 for the process.

If the board rules against you, the next step is court. Under section 40-3-25, an appeal from the board's decision must be taken within 30 days after the final ruling. You give notice to the board secretary and the circuit court clerk and post a bond approved by the clerk. A jury demand has to be filed within 10 days after the appeal is taken.

The statute also says you must pay the taxes due, measured on the prior year's assessment, before they turn delinquent, or the court can dismiss the appeal unless you posted a supersedeas bond. Circuit court appeals cannot stop the collection of tax. A seller who plans to appeal and sell in the same year should keep that in mind.

What online tax services does Calhoun County offer?

The county's website lists online property tax payment by check or credit card, a GIS map with appraisal information searchable by owner or address, and a business personal property portal. You can also renew boat and manufactured home decals and business licenses online.

  • GIS mapping: pull up a parcel, see its appraisal and find who owns it.
  • Online tax payments: handy when a closing date is close and a bill is still open.
  • Manufactured home renewal: the page lists October and November as the renewal window.

The commission meets in the Ken Joiner Administration Building at 1702 Noble Street in Anniston. Calhoun County's Revenue Commissioner has its own tab on the county site, so start there for assessing questions.

How much recording tax applies when a Calhoun County house sells?

Alabama charges 50 cents for each $500 of value conveyed, or any fraction of it, when a deed is recorded, under section 40-22-1. On a $120,000 sale that works out to 240 units at 50 cents, or $120, before the probate office's separate recording fee.

The statute taxes only value above any mortgage on which the mortgage tax was already paid, so the number can be lower than the simple math. A deed also has to arrive with proof of the actual price paid, using a form the Department of Revenue provides, and the person signing attests to it. The county's probate office takes the recording and collects the tax.

What do Calhoun County sellers with a hard-to-sell house run into?

Most of the trouble comes from three things: a house that needs repairs, an estate with several heirs, or a rental that has sat empty. Each of them slows a standard listing, because an agent sale depends on an appraisal, a lender and a buyer who can wait.

  • Back taxes: Alabama taxes are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31, and unpaid accounts move on to a tax sale in the spring.
  • Improvements: reported additions change the assessment, so a seller who added a deck or garage should expect the value to move.
  • Rural parcels: 36.5 percent of residents live outside urban areas, so a good share of sales involve rural lots rather than city parcels.

A cash sale skips the lender and the appraisal gap. We buy houses in Calhoun County as they stand, and we can talk through unpaid tax during the first call.

Taxes are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31. The state timetable then runs: turned over to probate court in February, probate court meets in March, properties advertised in April and sold at tax sale in May.

How long do I have to appeal my Calhoun County assessment?

You have 30 days from the written valuation notice to protest to the Board of Equalization. After a final board decision, a circuit court appeal must be taken within another 30 days.

Who is the county seat of Calhoun County, Alabama?

Anniston is the county seat. It replaced Jacksonville after a state Supreme Court ruling in June 1900.

Do I owe property tax if I never got a bill in Calhoun County?

Yes. The Alabama Department of Revenue says Revenue Commissioners mail notices only as a courtesy, and you owe the tax whether you receive a statement or not.

Can I sell a Calhoun County house that still has taxes due?

Yes, in many cases. Open taxes are normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Call us with the parcel number and we will look at what is owed before talking about an offer.

Tallapoosa County by the numbers

Where is Tallapoosa County, Alabama?

Tallapoosa County lies in the east-central part of Alabama, in the Piedmont region, with Dadeville as the county seat and Alexander City as the largest city. It covers 766 square miles, of which 717 are land and 50 are water, so water makes up about 6.5 percent of the county.

The Tallapoosa River runs through it. Seven counties border it: Clay to the north, Randolph to the northeast, Chambers to the east, Lee to the southeast, Macon to the south, Elmore to the southwest and Coosa to the west. The county's own website advertises more than 850 miles of shoreline.

With that much water, a house near the shore is a different kind of parcel from an inland lot. If yours is one of them, ask the revenue office how the land and improvements were appraised.

What is the history of Tallapoosa County?

Tallapoosa County was created on December 18, 1832, from land the Creek ceded in the Treaty of Cusseta. Its first county seat was the Creek town of Okfuskee.

The Battle of Horseshoe Bend took place in 1814 on ground that later became part of the county, and it effectively ended the Creek War. Horseshoe Bend National Military Park is the protected area listed for the county. After the forced removal of the Creek in 1836 and 1837, a gold rush brought settlers and prospectors. In 1866 the county's southwest strip was detached and became part of the new Elmore County.

The name comes from the Tallapoosa River, and the county was drawn at a time when many Creek villages stood along its lower banks before removal. Sources give more than one possible meaning, and the Wikipedia entry notes both a Choctaw reading and a Muscogee one.

How many people and homes are in Tallapoosa County?

Which cities, towns and school districts are in Tallapoosa County?

The county has three cities, five towns and three census-designated places. The cities are Alexander City, Dadeville and Tallassee, and Tallassee extends into Elmore County.

  • Towns: Camp Hill, Daviston, Goldville, Jackson's Gap and New Site.
  • Census-designated places: Hackneyville, Our Town and Reeltown.
  • Public school districts: Alexander City Schools, Tallapoosa County Schools and the Tallassee City School District.

Three separate districts mean the school boundary can change from one road to the next. Buyers who care about schools will ask which district a house belongs to, so have the answer ready.

What roads cross Tallapoosa County?

U.S. Highway 280, which is also State Route 38, is the major federal route through the county. The state routes listed are 14, 22, 49, 50, 63, 120, 128 and 259.

The county's Wikipedia profile lists no interstate, so every route on it is a U.S. or state highway. When you describe a house to a buyer, name the nearest of these roads and the nearest town.

What is the Alexander City area, and why does it matter to a seller?

Tallapoosa County makes up the Alexander City micropolitan statistical area on its own. The federal Office of Management and Budget dropped that area in 2013 and then reinstated it effective July 2023, now covering Tallapoosa County alone and tied to the Columbus-Auburn-Opelika combined statistical area.

That classification changes how federal data is grouped. The county's 78.4 percent rural population means many sales involve acreage, outbuildings or private water and septic.

When are Tallapoosa County property taxes due?

Alabama sets property tax as due on October 1 and delinquent after December 31, and Tallapoosa County follows the state schedule. The Alabama Department of Revenue states that date pair directly.

A bill that reaches the delinquent stage can grow with penalties and interest. We could not confirm the Tallapoosa County penalty rate or the date its tax sale begins from an official county page we could open, so we do not state them here. Call the Revenue Commissioner's office for the payoff before you set a closing date, and ask them to put the figure in writing for the closing agent.

  • Ask for the current-year balance and any prior-year balance.
  • Ask whether the bill is in the previous owner's name.
  • Ask which exemptions are currently on the parcel.

How do I dispute a Tallapoosa County property value?

File a written protest with the County Board of Equalization within 30 days of the written notice of valuation. That deadline comes from the Alabama Department of Revenue, which cites Code of Alabama sections 40-3-20, 40-3-24 and 40-3-25.

The office, hearing dates and forms are set locally. Because we could not open a Tallapoosa County page listing them, ask the Revenue Commissioner's office what the board requires. Bring a recent appraisal, repair estimates or comparable sales with you if you think the value is too high.

How does a cash sale work in Tallapoosa County?

A cash sale in Tallapoosa County follows the same steps as any Alabama sale, minus the lender. You send details about the house, receive a written offer, choose a closing date, and a title company clears any lien and tax balance from the proceeds.

That can help when a house has deferred repairs, a lapsed tenant, or heirs who live out of state. It also removes the wait for a lender's appraisal.

How has the Tallapoosa County population changed over time?

The county counted 35,074 people in 1950 and 33,840 in 1970, then climbed to 38,766 in 1980 and 41,475 in 2000. Since then it has stayed close to 41,000, with 41,616 in 2010 and 41,311 in 2020.

Smaller places inside the county include the unincorporated communities of Andrew Jackson, Bulgers, Cherokee Bluffs, Church Hill, Dudleyville, Fosheeton and Frog Eye. A buyer searching by one of those names may not find your house under a city name, so use the community name in your listing details.

What do Tallapoosa County sellers usually face?

Sellers in a county with a falling population, a median age of 46.4 and 22.5 percent of residents aged 65 or older often face estate sales and downsizing. The census figures describe the county as a whole, so a given street may differ.

  • Estate and heir sales, especially where a parent owned the house for decades.
  • Rental houses in a market with a 9.0 percent rental vacancy rate.
  • Rural parcels that need survey, access or septic answers before closing.
  • Houses held by older owners, in a county where 22.5 percent of residents were 65 or older in 2020.

Property taxes are due October 1 and are delinquent after December 31, according to the Alabama Department of Revenue.

Where is the Tallapoosa County seat?

Can I sell a Tallapoosa County house with back taxes owed?

Yes. The balance is normally paid out of the sale proceeds at closing, so get a payoff figure from the Revenue Commissioner's office first.

Where is Cullman County, Alabama?

Cullman County is in north central Alabama, with the city of Cullman serving as both county seat and largest city. It covers 755 square miles, 735 of them land and 20 water.

Morgan County lies to the north, Marshall to the northeast, Blount to the east, Walker to the southwest, Winston to the west and Lawrence to the northwest. How was Cullman County founded?

The Alabama legislature organized Cullman County on January 24, 1877 from parts of Blount, Morgan and Winston counties and named it for Colonel John G. Cullmann. The act set March 6, 1877 as the day residents would pick a county seat.

Two towns competed, Cullman and Milner, and Cullman won the vote 760 to 55. Before settlement, the area had been home for thousands of years to varied Indigenous cultures, and the Cherokee and Choctaw lived here at the time of European contact.

A more recent event shaped the county's building stock: the 2011 Cullman tornado struck on April 27, 2011 during the 2011 Super Outbreak. Repair history after a storm is something a buyer's inspector will ask about.

The county's growth curve is long. It had 6,355 people in 1880, 28,321 in 1910, 49,046 in 1950, a dip to 45,572 in 1960, then 61,642 in 1980, 77,483 in 2000 and 87,866 in 2020. The median age is 41.3, with 22.3 percent of residents under 18 and 18.9 percent aged 65 or older, so a good share of sellers are long-time owners with decades of equity in the house.

Which cities, towns and schools are in Cullman County?

Cullman County has four cities, nine towns and three public school systems: Cullman City Schools, Arab City Schools and Cullman County Schools.

  • Cities: Arab (mostly in Marshall County), Cullman, Good Hope and Hanceville.
  • Towns: Baileyton, Berlin, Colony, Dodge City, Fairview, Garden City (partly in Blount County), Holly Pond, South Vinemont and West Point.
  • Census-designated places: East Point and Joppa, the latter partly in Marshall County.

The county system covers unincorporated areas and every municipality except Arab and nearly all of Cullman. Wallace State Community College sits in Hanceville in the south end of the county, opened in 1966 and enrolls around 6,000 students. Private options in Cullman include Cullman Christian School, St. Bernard Preparatory School and Sacred Heart of Jesus Catholic Elementary School.

Which unincorporated communities sit in Cullman County?

Beyond the incorporated places, Cullman County has more than twenty named unincorporated communities, and many sellers live in one of them rather than in a city.

  • A to C: Arkadelphia, Battleground, Birdsong, Black Bottom, Bremen, Brooklyn, Bug Tussle, Corinth and Crane Hill.
  • D to L: Damascus, Jones Chapel and Logan.
  • P to W: Phelan, Simcoe, Spring Hill, Trimble, Vinemont, Walter, Welti, Wilburn and White City.

With 75.6 percent of residents outside urban areas, a house in one of these places is usually reached by a county road and falls under the county school system. Private schools add another layer, including Vinemont Christian Academy in South Vinemont, which serves pre-K through 12th grade.

What is different about alcohol rules in Cullman County?

Cullman County is classed as moist: the cities of Cullman, Good Hope and Hanceville allow alcohol sales and are wet, and the rest of the county is dry. It matters if you own a building that a restaurant or shop might use, since the answer depends on which side of the city line the parcel falls.

How does Alabama's annual equalization affect a Cullman County parcel?

Every Alabama county is under an annual reappraisal program that has the assessing official review one-quarter of the county each year. All property in a county gets looked at over a four-year cycle, and any new buildings found during that review get added for the next tax year.

The state says the goal is to smooth out large jumps in value and to keep the tax stream stable for schools, cities, counties and the state. If you want to see which year your area is reviewed, ask the Revenue Commissioner's office.

The Department of Revenue also says property owners should report new improvements or removals by December 31, and that re-roofing, minor repairs and painting do not trigger a new assessment.

How is recording tax split when a Cullman County house sells?

When a deed is recorded in Alabama, two-thirds of the privilege tax goes to the state treasury and one-third goes to the county treasury. The rate is 50 cents for each $500 of value conveyed or fraction of it, set by section 40-22-1.

The probate judge calculates the amount due from the actual purchase price, which must be attested on a Department of Revenue form. A deed that conveys property in two or more counties goes through the department, which sets the value in each county.

The statute includes a few exemptions: corrected deeds, deeds for nominal consideration that perfect title, and mortgage transfers where the mortgage tax is already paid. When a $240,000 sale is recorded, the tax is 480 units times 50 cents, or $240, with the probate office's recording fee added.

When are Cullman County taxes due and when do they go delinquent?

Property tax is due October 1 and delinquent after December 31. After that the state timetable runs February to the probate court, March for the probate court to meet, April for advertising and May for the tax sale.

  • You owe the tax even if no statement comes. Revenue Commissioners mail notices only as a courtesy.
  • A written protest of value goes to the Board of Equalization within 30 days of the valuation notice.
  • Owners 65 or older, permanently and totally disabled, or blind are exempt from the state portion once they claim the exemption.

For sellers with a deadline, the first quarter is the crunch. A house that closes in January or February may have an unpaid bill for the year just ended, which is the kind of item a closing agent looks for.

The legislature organized it on January 24, 1877. Cullman beat Milner in the county seat vote, 760 to 55.

Is Cullman County wet or dry?

It is moist. Cullman, Good Hope and Hanceville allow alcohol sales, and the rest of the county is dry.

How is a deed taxed in Cullman County?

Alabama charges 50 cents per $500 of value conveyed, and the probate office collects it when the deed is recorded.

Talladega County by the numbers

Where is Talladega County, Alabama, and how is it laid out?

Talladega County sits in the east-central part of Alabama, with the city of Talladega as both the county seat and the largest city. The Census Bureau lists 760 square miles in total, made up of 737 square miles of land and 24 square miles of water.

Six counties touch it: Calhoun to the north, Cleburne to the northeast, Clay to the east, Coosa to the south, Shelby to the southwest and St. Clair to the northwest. Choccolocco Creek and other streams drain the county, which lies in the Coosa River Valley and the Ridge-and-Valley Appalachians. Mount Cheaha, the highest point in Alabama, sits on the northeastern border with Cleburne County, and part of the Talladega National Forest falls inside Talladega County.

For a seller, that mix of creek bottoms, ridges and forest edge matters. Two houses a few miles apart can sit in very different flood, access and insurance situations, so a price from the other side of the county is a weak guide.

How did Talladega County start?

The county was established on December 18, 1832, from land the Creek had ceded, and the county seat was set at Talladega in 1834. Before that the area was home to the Abihka tribe of the Creek Confederacy.

The name comes from a Muscogee word usually translated as "Border Town," a reference to the line between Creek land and the lands of the Cherokee and Chickasaw. The county motto on its Wikipedia profile is "Something For Everyone."

What do the numbers say about housing in Talladega County?

The 2020 census counted 82,149 people and 37,948 housing units in Talladega County, and about one unit in eight was empty. The county's own population has barely moved in a decade, so most buyers of a Talladega County house are people already living nearby.

Which cities, towns and school systems are in Talladega County?

Talladega County has five cities and six towns, and Talladega County Schools is the public district named for the county. The cities are Childersburg, Lincoln, Oxford (partly in Calhoun County), Sylacauga and Talladega.

The towns are Bon Air, Munford, Oak Grove, Talladega Springs, Vincent (shared with Shelby and St. Clair counties) and Waldo. Fayetteville and Mignon are census-designated places, and the list of unincorporated communities runs from Eastaboga and Winterboro to Kentuck and Mardisville.

The county's own tax page lists extra school areas outside the cities: Childersburg, Fayetteville, Lincoln, Munford and Winterboro. Which one your house falls in changes the millage, which is covered below.

What roads and rail lines serve Talladega County?

Interstate 20 crosses the county, and U.S. Highways 78, 231 and 280 add the main north-south and east-west routes. State routes include 21, 34, 76, 77, 148, 202, 235 and 275.

Who sends the property tax bill in Talladega County?

The Talladega County Revenue Commissioner's office collects property tax, and the county site names Cindy Pennington as Revenue Commissioner. The pages we opened do not name a separate assessor office, so call the revenue office first about values and exemptions.

  • Taxes are due every year on October 1 and are delinquent after December 31.
  • Courtesy notices are usually mailed before October 1, but the owner must pay whether or not a bill arrives, even if it came in a prior owner's name.
  • The office does not take payments by phone.
  • Visa, Mastercard and Discover are accepted, with a convenience fee on every card payment.
  • Checks or money orders can be mailed to Talladega County Revenue Office, P.O. Box 1119, Talladega, AL 35161, payable to the Revenue Commissioner.

The Alabama Department of Revenue gives the same statewide dates: due October 1, delinquent after December 31.

How is a Talladega County tax bill calculated?

The county's calculator page gives three steps: find the assessed value, multiply by the millage rate, then subtract exemptions. Assessed value is the appraised value times a class percentage.

The class percentages shown on the county page are 30 percent for utility property, 20 percent for commercial, rental, industrial and other non-homestead property, and 10 percent for agricultural, forest and owner-occupied residential property. That split matters to sellers because a rental house is assessed at double the ratio of a home its owner lives in.

The county page labels one mill as one tenth of one penny. Rates change, so confirm the current figure with the office before you rely on any number here.

What would the tax look like on a sample Talladega County house?

On a $150,000 owner-occupied house inside the City of Talladega, the arithmetic from the county's formula gives $15,000 of assessed value and a bill of about $577.50 before exemptions. The same value in unincorporated District 1 at 29.0 mills would come to about $435.

A $150,000 rental house in the City of Talladega is assessed at 20 percent, or $30,000, which at 38.5 mills works out to about $1,155 before exemptions. These are worked examples using the county's published method, not a quote from the office, and your actual appraised value will differ.

What if I sell a Talladega County house with property tax still owed?

Back tax normally has to be settled at or before closing. A closing agent can ask the revenue office for the current balance and pay it from the sale proceeds.

Waiting past December 31 means the bill is delinquent. The county page we read does not spell out the penalty rate or the date the county starts its tax sale process, so ask the revenue office for the exact figures before you plan around them.

How do I appeal a Talladega County value?

You file a written protest with the County Board of Equalization, and the state says owners have 30 days after receiving written notice of valuation. The Alabama Department of Revenue points to Code of Alabama sections 40-3-20, 40-3-24 and 40-3-25 for the process.

We could not confirm a Talladega County board schedule or hearing location from an opened page, so ask the revenue office when you receive your notice. A notice you ignore for 30 days can lock in a value you think is too high.

What do Talladega County sellers usually run into?

With 58.7 percent of residents living in rural areas, many Talladega County houses sit outside a city lot, which can bring septic, well and road-access questions into a sale. These are the situations that most often complicate a sale in any county, and they apply here too.

  • Inherited houses with several heirs and an unpaid tax bill in a parent's name.
  • Rentals that went vacant, in a county with a 9.2 percent rental vacancy rate.
  • Houses with deferred repairs that may not satisfy a lender's appraisal.

Lee County by the numbers

What is Lee County, Alabama, and how did it take shape?

Lee County is in east central Alabama along the Georgia line, with Opelika as the county seat and Auburn as the largest city. The legislature created it on December 5, 1866, out of pieces of Macon, Tallapoosa, Chambers and Russell counties.

The choice of seat was settled by an election in which Opelika beat Auburn and Salem. In 1923 the county swapped land with Russell County so that the newly merged Phenix City would not straddle the county line, which is why the southern end of Lee County is a narrow panhandle around Marvyn. Even so, the city limits of Phenix City still reach into the southeast corner of Lee.

The county covers 616 square miles, 608 of them land. It sits on the fall line between the Piedmont to the north and the Gulf coastal plain to the south, so the northern townships are hillier than the southern ones.

How big is Lee County and what does the housing mix look like?

The 2020 census counted 174,241 people in Lee County, and the Census Bureau estimates 189,881 for 2025. The median age was 31.4, which fits a county built around a university.

Nearly 42% of occupied homes are rented, a large share of the housing stock. If you own a house that students or short-term tenants have lived in, the condition of the property after years of rental use is often the main thing a buyer prices in.

What drives the Lee County economy?

Education is the anchor. Lee County is home to Auburn University, a large public university, and to Southern Union State Community College, a two-year degree and technical school with a campus in Opelika.

The county is crossed by Interstate 85. Other main roads include U.S. 280, U.S. 80, U.S. 29 and U.S. 431, and freight moves on CSX and Norfolk Southern rail lines. Auburn University Regional Airport is also inside the county.

A seasonal rhythm follows the academic calendar. Leases tend to turn over with semesters, and an owner who wants to sell a rental often has to think about timing around tenants. That is one reason sellers here ask about quick closings and as-is purchases.

Which school systems and communities does Lee County include?

Lee County has four public school districts: Auburn City Schools, Lee County Schools, Opelika City Schools and Phenix City Public Schools.

  • Cities: Auburn, Opelika (county seat), Phenix City (partly in Russell County) and Smiths Station.
  • Towns: Loachapoka, Notasulga (partly in Macon County) and Waverly (partly in Chambers County).
  • Unincorporated communities include Beauregard, Beans Mill, Chewacla, Gold Hill, Salem and Marvyn.

Municipal boundaries change the bill you receive, because Alabama property tax combines county, municipal and school district levies. A house in an Auburn address and a house in an unincorporated part of the county can have very different carrying costs even at the same price.

When is Lee County property tax due, and what happens after it is late?

Lee County property taxes are due starting October 1 and become delinquent after December 31. The Alabama Department of Revenue shows the statewide sequence: delinquent January 1, handed to probate court in February, advertised in April, and sold in May.

The Lee County Revenue Commissioner's office runs the collection side from offices in Opelika and Auburn. Its website lists a few current items worth knowing:

  • A notice dated November 2, 2026 says a vendor error kept some property tax notices from being mailed on schedule, and that the missing notices would be mailed by Wednesday, November 4, 2026.
  • Checks to the office should be written to the Lee County Revenue Commissioner or Oline W. Price.
  • The offices do not process titles after 4 p.m.

A late notice does not change the legal due date. If yours has not arrived, call the office instead of waiting for it.

How does a Lee County property value appeal work?

An owner who thinks the assessed value is too high goes to the county Board of Equalization first, and the Lee County government posts a Board of Equalization page under its appraisal department. The deadlines are set by state law, so confirm each date with the county each year.

After the board decides, section 40-3-25 of the Code of Alabama allows an appeal to circuit court within 30 days of the board's final decision. The appeal papers go to both the board secretary and the circuit clerk, with a bond for costs. If the taxpayer wants a jury, the demand is due within 10 days after the appeal is taken.

The statute also says the taxpayer must pay the preceding year's taxes before they become delinquent, or post a supersedeas bond in double the taxes, or the court must dismiss the appeal. The circuit court cannot stop collection of taxes that are due.

Which exemptions apply to a Lee County home?

The state homestead exemption covers a single-family home that you own and live in as a primary residence on the first day of the tax year, on up to 160 acres. You file with the county office.

  • H-1: under 65 and not disabled, $4,000 of assessed value for state tax and $2,000 for county tax.
  • H-2: age 65 or older with adjusted gross income under $12,000, or permanently and totally disabled, with state tax exempt and $5,000 of assessed value exempt on the county side.
  • H-3: age 65 or older with net taxable income of $12,000 or less on a joint federal return, or totally disabled, exempt from all ad valorem taxes.
  • H-4: age 65 or older with income above $12,000, state tax exempt plus the regular county exemption.

An exemption applies to the owner-occupant, so when a house sells, the new owner has to claim it for themselves.

What happens when Lee County property tax is not paid?

Delinquent parcels go to the annual tax sale in May. After a tax sale, Alabama law lets the owner, heirs, a mortgagee or other interested party redeem the property within three years of the sale date, and a recorded lienholder gets additional time after written notice.

The statute, section 40-10-120, also lets a minor or a person under a legal disability redeem within one year after the disability ends. Redemption is not the same as having a clear title again, so a house with a recent tax sale in its history needs careful review before any closing.

For a seller this has a plain consequence. If the house is on the delinquent list, paying the balance before the May sale avoids the problem. If a sale already happened, the redemption clock is running, and payoff figures come from the Revenue Commissioner.

What do sellers face in Lee County after a tornado or heavy rental use?

On March 3, 2019, a series of tornadoes hit Lee County and killed 23 people, with the deaths and injuries centered on the Beauregard community southeast of the Auburn-Opelika area. Damaged and rebuilt homes from that event, and older rentals with deferred repairs, are two kinds of property that can be harder to sell the usual way.

  • Storm-damaged houses can be hard to sell on the open market because of repair and insurance questions.
  • Long-held student rentals can carry worn systems and tenants on staggered leases.
  • Inherited houses may have unpaid tax years and several heirs to coordinate.
  • Owners who live out of town can find it hard to manage repairs and showings from a distance.

We buy Lee County houses as they are. You can send photos and an address, and any unpaid taxes are settled from the proceeds at closing.

They are due beginning October 1 and must be paid by December 31 to avoid becoming delinquent.

Who collects property tax in Lee County?

The Lee County Revenue Commissioner, with offices in Opelika and Auburn. The county seat is Opelika.

When does Alabama hold its annual tax sale?

The state timetable puts the tax sale in May, after taxes turn delinquent on January 1 and are advertised in April.

How long can I redeem a house after a tax sale in Alabama?

Generally within three years of the sale date under Code of Alabama section 40-10-120, with extra time for some lienholders and for people under a legal disability.

Do renters affect how I sell a Lee County house?

They can. About 42% of occupied homes in the county are rented, so timing a sale around a lease is common, and as-is buyers can often work with that.

Cotton built the county's wealth through most of the 1800s, and government, rail, river shipping and military aviation carry it now. The boll weevil arrived in 1914 and hit the cotton harvest hard from 1915 on, and by the 1940s county farms earned more from cattle than from cotton.

Pintlala, Snowdoun and Mount Meigs are unincorporated communities in the county, so houses there sit outside city limits and a buyer should confirm which services and taxes apply.

Montgomery Public Schools serves most of the county, with its headquarters at 307 S. Decatur Street. Pike Road City School District runs the public schools in Pike Road, and the on-base school at Maxwell Air Force Base is operated by the Department of Defense Education Activity.

The county has one city, Montgomery, and two towns, Hope Hull and Pike Road. Unincorporated places include Ada, Cecil, Grady, Le Grand, Mathews, Pintlala, Ramer and Waugh. How do you appeal a Montgomery County assessment?

You appeal to the county Board of Equalization, and the county says the deadline is thirty days from the date printed on your notice. The Board of Equalization appeals page states that there is no filing fee.

  • No special form is required, but the Board wants an original signature.
  • Send the supporting papers with the appeal. The county names closing statements, appraisals, comparable sales and insurance values as examples.
  • An informal review before the deadline is available and the county recommends it.
  • Out-of-state agents may file, and an attorney is not required, but the agent must supply a signed authorization.

The county's own FAQ was written for tax year 2024, and it says comparable sales for that year came from October 1, 2022 through September 30, 2023. Check the current notice for the dates that apply to your year.

What homestead exemptions can lower a Montgomery County tax bill?

A deed is recorded with the judge of probate, and state law attaches a recordation tax of 50 cents for each $500 of value conveyed. The recording office asks for proof of the real price paid. The law adds a penalty of $100 or 25% of the tax due, whichever is greater, if someone intentionally withholds that proof after a request. A title or escrow company normally handles the paperwork, but you should know the rule exists.

If a tax bill is open at closing, ask the title company how it will be paid from proceeds. For a deceased owner's house, the personal representative has to be in place before anyone can sign a deed.

There is no fee. The county's Board of Equalization FAQ says filing an appeal costs nothing, though you must file within thirty days of the date on your notice.

They are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31, per the Alabama Department of Revenue. Unpaid accounts move toward a probate court process that ends in a tax sale in May.

The Board of Equalization, working with the county Appraisal Department. Real property appeals go to propertytaxappeals@mc-ala.org or (334) 832-1327.

Yes. Ask the county for the amount owed and the title company how it will be paid at closing. A cash buyer can often fold that payoff into the sale.

Where is Morgan County, Alabama, and what is in it?

Morgan County is in north-central Alabama along the Tennessee River, with Decatur as the county seat and largest city. It covers 599 square miles, of which 579 are land and 20 are water, according to the Census Bureau figures repeated on Wikipedia.

The territorial legislature created the county in 1818 from land the Cherokee ceded in the Treaty of Turkeytown, and first called it Cotaco County. In 1821 lawmakers changed the name to honor Revolutionary War General Daniel Morgan of Virginia.

The population has risen every decade on record. The census counted 5,263 residents in 1820, 100,043 in 1990 and 123,421 in 2020, a gain of 3.3% from 2010. For a seller, steady growth of that kind usually means a continuing pool of buyers, though it says nothing about any single house.

What deed tax applies when a Morgan County house sells?

Dale County by the numbers

Where is Dale County, Alabama, and how big is it?

Dale County sits in the southeast corner of Alabama, in the Wiregrass region, roughly forty miles from both Georgia and Florida. The county site gives its size as 561 square miles, and Wikipedia ranks it fifth-smallest in Alabama by land area.

Ozark is the county seat and the largest city. Pike, Barbour, Henry, Houston, Geneva and Coffee counties surround it. Dale County makes up the Ozark micropolitan area, which belongs to the larger Dothan-Ozark combined statistical area.

For a seller, the small footprint matters in a simple way. Houses in Ozark, Daleville, Level Plains and the farm towns all answer to one county revenue office and one probate office, so the paperwork path is the same wherever the house stands.

How did Dale County get its borders?

Alabama created Dale County on December 22, 1824, and it was far larger then. It once took in all of what became Coffee and Geneva counties plus a panhandle piece of Houston County.

The first county seat was Dale's Court House, now the town of Daleville. The seat moved to Newton in 1841 when Coffee County split off, then to Ozark in 1870 after a courthouse fire in 1869 and the creation of Geneva County. A small southeastern slice went to the new Houston County in 1903.

These boundary changes still show up in old deeds. A parcel description that mentions Newton or Dale's Court House can point to a title chain that predates the current lines, which is one reason title companies like to see a clean search before any closing in the county.

What do the numbers say about Dale County homes and residents?

The 2020 census counted 49,326 people in Dale County, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 49,912. Housing is split between owners and renters more evenly than in many Alabama counties.

How does Fort Rucker shape the Dale County housing market?

Most of Fort Rucker lies inside Dale County, and the county commission describes it as the home of Army Aviation and a primary training base for military helicopter pilots. The county site now lists the post as Fort Novosel.

Ozark and Daleville each border the installation. Military families move in and out on orders, and about 40 percent of occupied homes in the county are rented.

A seller who is moving on orders usually cannot wait through months of showings and repairs. A direct cash sale with a short closing date fits that schedule, and it removes the risk of holding a vacant house in another state.

Which cities and towns are in Dale County?

The county has five cities and seven towns, plus the Army post. Wikipedia and the county commission list the same communities.

  • Cities: Daleville, Dothan (partly in Houston and Henry counties), Enterprise (partly in Coffee County), Level Plains and Ozark.
  • Towns: Ariton, Clayhatchee, Grimes, Midland City, Napier Field, Newton and Pinckard.
  • Unincorporated places include Skipperville, Echo, Clopton, Kelly and Rocky Head.

Where a house sits decides which city rules apply to code enforcement, utilities and school zoning. A home in an unincorporated community answers mainly to the county.

Which school districts cover Dale County houses?

Most of the county is zoned to the Dale County School District, but four municipal systems carve out their own areas. Buyers ask about school zoning early, so a seller should know which one applies.

  • Dale County School District for most unincorporated areas
  • Daleville City Schools
  • Ozark City Schools
  • Enterprise City Schools and Dothan City Schools for the parts of those cities inside the county
  • Department of Defense Education Activity schools for elementary students living on Fort Rucker

Families on the post can choose Daleville, Enterprise or Ozark schools for the secondary grades, according to the Wikipedia article, which cites Military OneSource.

What roads connect Dale County to the rest of Alabama?

Two U.S. highways cross the county. U.S. 84 runs east and west, and U.S. 231 runs north and south through the Ozark area.

State routes 27, 37, 51, 85, 92, 123, 134, 248, 249 and 605 fill in the rest of the network. The county has no interstate, so commutes to Dothan and Enterprise rely on these routes.

When are Dale County property taxes due?

Alabama taxes are due October 1 and become delinquent after December 31, according to the state Department of Revenue. Dale County follows the statewide timetable.

  • October 1: taxes due
  • January 1: taxes delinquent
  • February: unpaid accounts turned over to the Probate Court
  • March: Probate Court meets
  • April: properties advertised for sale
  • May: tax sale

The county's Revenue department handles assessment and collection locally, and the Probate Office records deeds. A seller with an unpaid bill should ask the Revenue office for a payoff amount before setting a closing date.

What happens to property tax when a Dale County house sells?

The tax bill follows the property, not the person. Etowah County's published FAQ makes the point plainly for Alabama: delinquent taxes must be satisfied by whoever owns the property, even if they accrued before that owner bought it.

In practice the closing agent checks for open balances and pays them from the seller's proceeds, so a seller should ask the Revenue office for a current payoff figure before setting a closing date.

Homestead status is worth a question at a sale. Etowah County's FAQ says the regular homestead exemption is for a principal residence and can be claimed year round, so a buyer who moves in should ask the Revenue office how to claim it.

What does it cost to record a deed in Dale County?

Alabama charges a recording privilege tax of fifty cents for each $500 of value on a deed, under Alabama Code section 40-22-1. The probate office collects it when the deed is filed.

The same section requires proof of the actual purchase price, and the Department of Revenue provides a form for that. A $150,000 sale works out to 300 units of $500, so the tax is $150 before the probate judge's separate recording fee. Two-thirds of the tax goes to the state and one-third to the county.

Knowingly leaving out the price proof after the office asks for it can bring a penalty of $100 or 25 percent of the tax, whichever is greater.

Can you appeal a Dale County property value?

Yes. A property owner who disagrees with a valuation starts with the Revenue office, then goes to the county Board of Equalization.

Under section 40-3-25 as printed in the 2022 Alabama Code, an appeal of a board ruling goes to circuit court within 30 days of the board's final decision. The taxpayer still has to pay the tax before it turns delinquent, or the appeal can be dismissed. Check the current code and the Revenue office for the exact protest dates, since the filing window for the board itself was not confirmed here.

What do sellers with tax trouble in Dale County usually face?

Most calls involve one of a few situations. Each has a different clock.

  • An inherited house with several years of unpaid taxes and no one living there
  • A rental with repairs the owner cannot afford and a tenant already gone
  • A military family leaving on orders with a house still on the market
  • A house heading toward the May tax sale after a January delinquency

A cash buyer can pay the back taxes at closing and take the house as it stands. That matters most when the property is close to the spring sale calendar.

October 1. They become delinquent after December 31, and unpaid accounts move to the Probate Court in February, with a tax sale in May, according to the Alabama Department of Revenue.

Who assesses property in Dale County?

The Dale County Revenue office handles assessment and collection locally, and the Probate Office records deeds. The county commission site lists both departments.

Do I owe back taxes if I inherit a Dale County house?

Yes. Alabama taxes follow the property, so unpaid years must be settled by the current owner. The balance is usually paid from sale proceeds at closing.

How much is the deed tax on a Dale County sale?

Fifty cents per $500 of value under Alabama Code 40-22-1. A $150,000 sale carries $150 in tax, plus the probate recording fee.

Is Fort Rucker inside Dale County?

Most of it is. The county commission describes the installation as bordering Ozark and Daleville, and Wikipedia says the vast majority lies within Dale County.

Where is Russell County, Alabama?

Russell County is the easternmost county in Alabama, on the Georgia line across the Chattahoochee River from Columbus. Phenix City is the county seat and largest city, and the county forms part of the Columbus, Georgia and Alabama metropolitan area.

It covers 647 square miles, with 641 of land and 6.1 of water. Lee County lies to the north, and Barbour, Bullock and Macon counties touch it inside Alabama. Muscogee, Chattahoochee and Stewart counties in Georgia sit across the state line.
